# Collaborative Architecture

> Collaborative Architecture is an internationally award-winning studio headquartered in Mumbai, India, with a satellite studio in Riyadh, KSA. Our projects evolve out of a meaningful convergence of people, places, culture, climate, ecology and economics.

## Key facts

- Founded: 2004, in Mumbai
- Principals: Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, co-founders
- Studios: Mumbai Studio, Mumbai, India; Riyadh Studio, Riyadh, KSA
- Disciplines: Architecture, interior architecture, urban design and infrastructure, narrative environments and installations, products and objects, design and behavioral mapping
- Recognition: 60 awards, honors and international shortlists, 30 of them international
- Exhibitions: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York; Museum of Craft and Design, San Francisco; The National Gallery of Modern Art, Mumbai
- Research: Collaborative Lab: design research, policy advocacy, epistemologies and architectural cartographies
- Contact: For new projects and collaborations: enquiry@collaborativearchitecture.com; Vendors and suppliers, kindly use the contact form

## Expertise

- [Architecture](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/architecture/): Designed for enduring relevance
- [Interior Architecture](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/interior-architecture/): Architecture at the human scale
- [Urban Design and Infrastructure](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/urban-design-and-infrastructure/): Infrastructure as a framework for urban life
- [Narrative Environments and Installations](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/narrative-environments-and-installations/): Space as a medium for storytelling
- [Products and Objects](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/products-and-objects/): Objects emerging from architectural inquiry
- [Design and Behavioral Mapping](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/design-and-behavioral-mapping/): Human behavior as a generator of space

# The studio

> Collaborative Architecture is an internationally award-winning studio headquartered in Mumbai, India, with a satellite studio in Riyadh, KSA. Our projects evolve out of a meaningful convergence of people, places, culture, climate, ecology and economics.

## Key facts

- Founded: 2004, in Mumbai
- Principals: Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, co-founders
- Studios: Mumbai Studio, Mumbai, India; Riyadh Studio, Riyadh, KSA
- Disciplines: Architecture, interior architecture, urban design and infrastructure, narrative environments and installations, products and objects, design and behavioral mapping
- Recognition: 60 awards, honors and international shortlists, 30 of them international
- Exhibitions: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York; Museum of Craft and Design, San Francisco; The National Gallery of Modern Art, Mumbai
- Research: Collaborative Lab: design research, policy advocacy, epistemologies and architectural cartographies
- Contact: For new projects and collaborations: enquiry@collaborativearchitecture.com; Vendors and suppliers, kindly use the contact form

## Principals

### Lalita Tharani, Co-founder and Principal

Lalita Tharani’s work focuses on how people perceive and use space, on materials and on the adoption of new technology, and she leads material research and technology at Collaborative Lab. She brought the studio’s Black-Box Series of experimental installations to life with Levitation, shown at the DX Show in New Delhi in 2019. Lalita is an advocate for women’s leadership and diversity in architecture. She received the WADe Role Model Award and the AIS Keystone Award in 2016, and she has served on juries and spoken at design events in India and abroad.

### Mujib Ahmed, Co-founder and Principal

Mujib Ahmed brings conceptual depth to the studio’s major projects and competitions and leads complex, multidisciplinary teams across countries. He leads academic research at Collaborative Lab and, with Lalita Tharani and colleagues, contributed to the Design Policy for the State of Kerala, the first such policy adopted by an Indian state. Mujib writes The Collaborative Logs, a monthly newsletter on architecture, research and speculative futures.

## Selected honors

- 2022–23: Peace Pavilion, exhibited at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York, and the Museum of Craft and Design, San Francisco
- 2021: National Unity Pavilion, one of the three winning entries, Notions of India international competition
- 2019: The Souk, winner of the Dubai Design Week installation program
- 2017: Cascadia, with J. MAYER H., finalist for the BCDA Iconic Tower, Manila
- 2016: Reflected Topography, winner of OFFICE NEXT, international workspace category
- 2015: Reflected Topography, IES Illumination Awards, Merit Award
- 2017: Finalist, two-stage international competition for the Indian National War Museum, Government of India

# Total Design | From human insight to spatial intelligence: the approach of Collaborative Architecture

Total Design is our integrated approach to the built environment, connecting every scale of intervention, from urban systems to the finest architectural detail, and every stage of a project, from initial inquiry to long-term performance. It brings design, technology, human experience and material intelligence into a coherent whole, guided by four principles.

## Innovative

We embrace new technologies, materials and processes where they create frameworks for meaningful engagement with the people who experience our work. Innovation informs every stage of our process, from interpreting the brief to the engineering and production of architecture. Through our research platform, we investigate emerging technologies, material systems and fabrication methods alongside the enduring intelligence of vernacular practices. Each is evaluated for its contextual relevance, technical performance and contribution to human experience, enabling us to advance architectural possibilities with purpose, rigor and a future-proof design.

## Responsive

We shape each project in dialogue with its context, responding to its site, climate, culture, client and community. We approach each project as an inquiry into the interplay of site, climate, culture and human needs. Through close dialogue with clients and communities, we reconcile aspirations, resources and constraints to develop context-responsive architecture. Participatory engagement informs our process across scales, grounding each intervention in its setting while seeking to enrich the lives and environments it touches.

## Performative

We design for environmental responsibility, human well-being and enduring value. We design buildings and systems for enduring performance, integrating environmental responsibility, resource efficiency and human well-being. Passive strategies, responsible material choices and adaptable planning inform buildings that perform efficiently, respond to changing needs and retain their value over time. Our design longevity strategies anchor human health and well-being at the center of environmental performance.

## Collaborative

We bring global expertise and diverse perspectives into the making of each project. We bring clients, users and a global network of specialists into the design process as active collaborators. By bringing diverse disciplines and perspectives into dialogue, we challenge established assumptions, synthesize collective knowledge and discover more appropriate architectural solutions.

## A case for future-proof design

Artificial intelligence and new ways of working are changing how we live and work faster than most buildings can adapt. Spaces become outdated and expensive to refit. Our research-led approach explores how spatial adaptability and enduring design intent can extend a building’s useful life, reducing obsolescence and the need for resource-intensive refits. We see the capacity to evolve as a fundamental measure of architectural sustainability.

# Expertise

We work at every scale, from urban systems to the finest architectural detail. We serve private, corporate and public clients through our integrated approach to the built environment.

## [Architecture](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/architecture/)

Designed for enduring relevance. Collaborative Architecture designs buildings and campuses for education, work, research, culture, worship, and civic life.

## [Interior Architecture](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/interior-architecture/)

Architecture at the human scale. Interior architecture shapes how architecture is experienced at close range. We conceive interiors as an extension of the building, where materiality, light, acoustics, proportion, and spatial relationships inform the experience of place.

## [Urban Design and Infrastructure](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/urban-design-and-infrastructure/)

Infrastructure as a framework for urban life. Infrastructure shapes how cities function, connect, and evolve. From bridges and transit networks to riverfronts and public spaces, we explore how large-scale interventions can extend beyond utility to become civic landmarks and sources of collective identity.

## [Narrative Environments and Installations](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/narrative-environments-and-installations/)

Space as a medium for storytelling. We design environments that communicate through spatial experience. Retail spaces, galleries, museums, and experience centers become narratives shaped by sequence, light, material, sound, and movement.

## [Products and Objects](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/products-and-objects/)

Objects emerging from architectural inquiry. Many of our products originate in the specific demands of architectural projects, translating spatial concepts into objects with an independent design identity.

## [Design and Behavioral Mapping](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/design-and-behavioral-mapping/)

Human behavior as a generator of space. We investigate how people live, work, interact, move, and occupy space before design begins.

# Architecture

Designed for enduring relevance. An expertise of Collaborative Architecture.

Collaborative Architecture designs buildings and campuses for education, work, research, culture, worship, and civic life. Each project begins with an investigation of its context, users, and economic realities, informing architecture that performs over time and adapts to evolving technologies and patterns of living. We treat the brief as a point of departure, using research and critical inquiry to uncover possibilities beyond its conventional boundaries.

## Performance | Measured over time

We evaluate architecture through its performance over time—from energy efficiency, daylight, and natural ventilation to the social life of public spaces and the capacity to accommodate change. Working within constraints, including limited budgets, we see resourcefulness as a catalyst for innovation, translating rigorous design thinking into buildings that deliver lasting value.

# Interior Architecture

Architecture at the human scale. An expertise of Collaborative Architecture.

Interior architecture shapes how architecture is experienced at close range. We conceive interiors as an extension of the building, where materiality, light, acoustics, proportion, and spatial relationships inform the experience of place. Through behavioral mapping, spatial analysis, and collaborative workshops, we translate our clients’ aspirations and patterns of use into tailored environments. Our work spans workplaces, restaurants, hotels, residences, showrooms, and experience centers, integrating every layer of the interior—from lighting and furniture to the sequences through which spaces are encountered.

## Designed in collaboration

Our clients are active partners in the design process, bringing an understanding of their lives, ambitions, and operations that informs our design expertise. We synthesize these insights with research into human behavior, materials, environmental performance, and cost to create spaces that respond holistically to their users and purpose. Designed for a long life cycle, our interiors prioritize durable materials, efficient systems, adaptability, and reduced operating costs.

## Projects

- [Apartment by the Bay](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/apartment-by-the-bay/): Private residence, Mumbai, 2014
- [Reflected Topography](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/reflected-topography/): Bearys Global Research Triangle, Bengaluru, 2014

- [Inverted Topography](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/inverted-topography/): Mezban restaurant, Kozhikode, 2010
- [50th Cross Road](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/50th-cross-road/): Show apartment, PVS Developers, Kerala, 2020

# Urban Design and Infrastructure

Infrastructure as a framework for urban life. An expertise of Collaborative Architecture.

Infrastructure shapes how cities function, connect, and evolve. From bridges and transit networks to riverfronts and public spaces, we explore how large-scale interventions can extend beyond utility to become civic landmarks and sources of collective identity. Our proposals include work developed with Henning Larsen for the Musi River in Hyderabad and with J. MAYER H. for a national landmark in Manila.

## Livability, ecology, and cultural identity

Our urban work examines the interplay of livability, ecology, mobility, and cultural context. We seek opportunities to restore natural systems, strengthen urban connections, and create public realms that respond to the character of their surroundings. By integrating infrastructure with the social and ecological fabric of a place, we aim to shape cities that are more connected, resilient, and meaningful to the communities they serve.

## Projects

- [The Iconic Gateway](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-gateway/): Diyar Al Muharraq, Bahrain, 2023
- [The Measured City](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-measured-city/): National Pavilion of the UAE, Venice Biennale 2027, 2026

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/urban-design-and-infrastructure/

# Narrative Environments and Installations

Space as a medium for storytelling. An expertise of Collaborative Architecture.

We design environments that communicate through spatial experience. Retail spaces, galleries, museums, and experience centers become narratives shaped by sequence, light, material, sound, and movement. Working with brands and cultural institutions, we translate products, ideas, and histories into immersive experiences that unfold as visitors move through space. Our collaborations include MillerKnoll, Titan, Hyundai, Stanley, and Moroso.

## Temporary architecture as a laboratory

Pavilions, prototypes, and installations provide a platform to test architectural ideas at full scale, exploring their spatial, material, and experiential potential before they inform permanent environments. Prototype N[ON] for Moroso and Wedge-1 for Stanley exemplify this experimental approach. Through the Black-Box Series, Collaborative Lab extends this inquiry into spatial speculations that challenge conventions and explore new architectural possibilities.

## Projects

- [Rasa Totem](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/rasa-totem/): With Riyas Komu, Bengaluru

# Products and Objects

Objects emerging from architectural inquiry. An expertise of Collaborative Architecture.

Many of our products originate in the specific demands of architectural projects, translating spatial concepts into objects with an independent design identity. Huddle seating and the 53 light, developed for Reflected Topography, and the Thousand Moons fixtures at Mezban exemplify this process. Supported by Collaborative Lab’s material research and prototyping, these explorations extend into furniture, lighting, objects, and jewelry.

## From cultural reference to contemporary production

Drawing from the murals and eroded landscapes of AlUla, Saudi Arabia, the Cliff Chair and Ripple jewelry collection translate cultural and geological references into contemporary forms. The Clip Chair explores the interplay of polycarbonate and bent plywood across different finishes and configurations. Through ongoing collaborations with Italian manufacturers, we continue to develop furniture that connects design research, material experimentation, and the possibilities of production.

## Projects

- [Rasa Totem](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/rasa-totem/): With Riyas Komu, Bengaluru

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/products-and-objects/

# Design and Behavioral Mapping

Human behavior as a generator of space. An expertise of Collaborative Architecture.

We investigate how people live, work, interact, move, and occupy space before design begins. Through behavioral mapping, organizational analysis, workshops, and spatial audits, we translate patterns of use into evidence-based insights that shape the brief and inform design decisions. This process grounds our work in the needs, aspirations, and behaviors of the people who inhabit the spaces we create.

## From mapping to implementation

Our methodology combines three complementary approaches. Organizational mapping examines team structures, workflows, and patterns of collaboration. Participatory workshops bring future users into the design process, integrating their experiences and aspirations. Spatial audits assess existing environments, materials, and patterns of use to identify what works and where improvements are needed.

The same integrated team supports implementation through procurement, vendor coordination, document control, and payment certification. This continuity connects research and design intent with project delivery, helping ensure that the completed environment reflects the approved design.

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/expertise/design-and-behavioral-mapping/

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/apartment-by-the-bay/ -->

# Apartment by the Bay

Private residence, Mumbai. Mumbai, India, 2014. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Located in Cuffe Parade, Mumbai, Apartment by the Bay is a 180-square-meter family residence completed in 2014. Set within one of the city’s sought-after residential buildings, the apartment opens to panoramic views of the Arabian Sea. The Interior Architecture balances a restrained minimalist language with a highly personalized approach, translating the clients’ refined aesthetic sensibilities and outgoing lifestyles into a home shaped around their individual needs.

## Key facts

- Location: Cuffe Parade, Mumbai, India
- Client: Private
- Typology: Residential, Interior
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2014
- Area: 180 m²
- Lighting design: Collaborative Architecture

## Minimal, and personal

Designed for a young family, the residence explores how minimalism can accommodate individuality without sacrificing spatial clarity. Rather than imposing a predetermined design language, the interiors are customized around the family’s distinct habits, preferences, and patterns of living. The result is an understated yet expressive domestic environment in which considered simplicity provides the framework for personal identity and everyday life.

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/reflected-topography/ -->

# Reflected Topography

Bearys Global Research Triangle, Bengaluru. Bengaluru, India, 2014. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Reflected Topography is the public lobby of the Bearys Global Research Triangle, a research and development campus in Bengaluru housing facilities for international companies. Within a 32 × 32-meter hall, the project integrates reception, waiting, relaxation, circulation, and private meeting spaces into a unified architectural experience. Conceived as an extension of the campus’s research-driven ethos, the design explores how structure, light, and spatial organization can transform a multifunctional interior into a coherent and dynamic public realm.

## Key facts

- Location: Bengaluru, India
- Client: Bearys Group
- Typology: Workplace, Research campus
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2014
- Area: 1,200 m² public lobby
- Certification: LEED Platinum (campus)
- Lighting design: Collaborative Architecture
- 32 × 32 m column-free lobby under a waffle slab
- 53 custom-designed lights

## Light as an extension of structure

The existing waffle slab provides the generative pattern for 53 custom-designed lights, integrated into its coffers to unite architectural structure and illumination. Radiating from a nine-meter-high central column clad in Corian panels, the lighting creates an overhead landscape that gives the interior its defining identity. Glazing along two sides draws daylight deep into the space, while a building management system with DALI lighting controls responds to available daylight to reduce energy consumption. The result is an integrated system in which structure, material, and light are conceived as interdependent elements.

## Furniture as a spatial landscape

Custom-designed seating clusters translate the geometry of the ceiling into an undulating landscape at eye level. Beyond furnishing the lobby, these formations establish informal meeting places and encourage social interaction, extending the architectural concept into the experience of occupation. Cantilevered meeting rooms added to the existing mezzanine accommodate private meetings while optimizing the available area and creating additional revenue potential for the client. Recognized for its integration of workplace functionality and architectural expression, the project won the international workplace category at OFFICE NEXT in 2016 and received recognition from the IES Illumination Awards and the International Design Awards (IDA) in 2015.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2016: OFFICE NEXT, International Workspace category, Winner
- 2015: International Design Awards (IDA), Honorable Mention (https://idesignawards.com/winners/zoom.php?eid=9-8849-15)
- 2015: IES Illumination Awards, Section Award
- 2015: IES Illumination Awards, Merit Award

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/house-of-cantilevers/ -->

# House of Cantilevers

Private residence, Kerala. Kerala, India. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Overlooking a scenic valley in South India, the House of Cantilevers is conceived as a sequence of projecting volumes that engage with the terrain while minimizing the building’s footprint. Organized across three levels on a contoured site, the 1,100-square-meter residence integrates spatial planning, structural expression, and passive climate strategies. The architecture balances expansive views with environmental responsiveness and a carefully considered hierarchy of domestic spaces.

## Key facts

- Location: Kerala, India
- Client: Private
- Typology: Residential
- Status: Under construction
- Area: 1,100 m²
- Consultants: Tekton Consultants (MEP); Prakrthi Living Environment (landscape)
- 6 bedrooms cantilevered toward the valley
- 8–9 m length of each cantilever

## Six bedrooms that reach over the valley

The primary public spaces occupy the mid-entry level, the bedrooms are positioned above, and service and ancillary spaces are accommodated in the basement. All six bedrooms project 8 to 9 meters toward the valley, giving the residence its name and extending the experience of the landscape into the private domain.

The curved plan, passive shading devices, semi-enclosed courts, and alternating projecting and recessed volumes respond to the sun’s path, helping to moderate thermal exposure and maintain interior comfort. These strategies shape the building’s form while grounding its spatial organization in the conditions of the site.

The project’s structural ambition is matched by its sensitivity to the cultural and domestic expectations of the family. Designed for a traditional Muslim family in Kerala, the residence maintains clear boundaries between public and private domains while adopting an open-plan approach. The result reconciles a traditional hierarchy of spaces with a contemporary architectural language, allowing openness, privacy, and connection to the landscape to coexist.

## In print

- 2015 Oct: GID (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2015-10-gid-studio-profile.pdf)
- 2015 Oct: Gulf News, Sophisticated, personalised homes (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2015-10-gulf-news-house-of-cantilevers.pdf)
- 2015 Nov: Trends (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2015-11-home-and-design-trends-house-of-cantilevers.pdf)
- 2016 Jan: Society Interiors, Icon (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2016-01-society-interiors-icon-issue.pdf)
- 2016 Jul: Inside Outside, interview (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2016-07-inside-outside-interview-with-the-principals.pdf)

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/cascadia/ -->

# Cascadia

BCDA Iconic Tower, Manila, with J. MAYER H. Metro Manila, Philippines, 2017. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Cascadia was a finalist entry in the two-stage international competition for the BCDA Iconic Tower, organized by the Government of the Philippines and the Bonifacio Development Authority in Manila. Designed by Collaborative Architecture in collaboration with J. MAYER H. und Partner Architekten, Berlin, the 40,000-square-meter proposal envisioned a national landmark for Bonifacio’s emerging central business district, transforming a former military site into a contemporary urban destination. The project explores how a high-rise development can extend beyond commercial functions to support cultural identity, public life, resilience, and sustainability.

## Key facts

- Location: Bonifacio, Metro Manila, Philippines
- Client: Government of the Philippines and BCDA
- Typology: Mixed use, Tower
- Status: Finalist, two-stage international competition
- Year: 2017
- Area: 40,000 m²
- In collaboration with: J. MAYER H. und Partner, Architekten, Berlin
- Consultants: Web Structures (structure); Element Design Studio (landscape); Building Façade Group (façade); Bo Steiber Lighting Design (lighting); Environmental Design Solutions (sustainability); Meinhardt (services); Rider Levett Bucknall (cost)
- 124 m tall tower

## A vertical park of stacked volumes

The tower is conceived as a three-dimensional composition of stacked volumes, recalling the stone piles historically used as markers of place and orientation. These distinct forms are brought together as a vertical landscape, accommodating spaces for planting, work, leisure, retail, and culture. The intervals between the volumes become elevated terraces, creating opportunities for public interaction and recreation above the city.

The composition also draws on the Philippine national flag as a symbol of unity and peace. Rather than treating the tower as an isolated object, Cascadia proposes an interconnected sequence of programs and spaces, establishing a new urban environment within the evolving business district.

## A cultural destination at ground level

At the base, an urban park establishes the project’s principal civic interface. Conceived to accommodate a significant collection of public art by artists from the Philippines and abroad, the park positions the landmark as a cultural destination as well as an architectural one. Its landscape connects with the planned linear park along Bonifacio’s east–west axis, extending the district’s public realm and integrating the project into the wider urban framework.

The proposal balances its ambition as a national landmark with the practical demands of privately financed development, including cost optimization, operational efficiency, and flexible leasable floor plates. Cascadia thus explores how commercial viability and civic purpose can coexist, allowing architecture and landscape to contribute to a broader expression of national identity.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2017: Finalist, BCDA Iconic Tower, two-stage international competition, with J. MAYER H.

## In print

- 2017: BluPrint, special issue (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2017-bluprint-special-issue-cascadia.pdf)
- 2018 Dec: Society Interiors, studio profile (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2018-12-society-interiors-studio-profile.pdf)

## Online

- 2020 Apr: BluPrint (https://bluprint.onemega.com/collaborative-architecture-key-projects-of-the-decade/)

## Writing

- 2026 Aug: The Collaborative Logs: The Narrative Environment (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/narrative-environment-re-imagining-contemporary-retail-mujib-ahmed-9w1rf)

## Credit for publications

Cascadia, Metro Manila. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/cascadia/)

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-gateway/ -->

# The Iconic Gateway

Diyar Al Muharraq, Bahrain. Muharraq, Bahrain, 2023. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Iconic Gateway marks the entrance to Diyar Al Muharraq in Bahrain. Conceived as both a pedestrian bridge and a landmark within the emerging urban landscape, it establishes a distinctive threshold to the new city. Drawing inspiration from Bahrain’s maritime heritage and the interlocking arches of the Diyar identity, the design synthesizes cultural symbolism with structural innovation, engineered to respond to the climatic demands of the Gulf.

Two 65-meter steel pylons support a cable-suspended footbridge, creating a distinctive silhouette that marks the entrance to the township.

## Key facts

- Location: Diyar Al Muharraq, Bahrain
- Client: Diyar Al Muharraq
- Typology: Infrastructure, Civic
- Status: Competition proposal
- Year: 2023
- Structure: Web Structures, Ramboll
- 65 m height of each steel pylon
- 165 m clear span
- Vernacular intelligence wind catchers and screens

## Engineering for climate and comfort

The bridge integrates structural clarity with environmental responsiveness. A double layer of stainless-steel solar screens, informed by the region’s mashrabiya traditions, filters heat and glare while providing shelter from harsh weather. Timber decking and a radiant cooling system address pedestrian comfort during Bahrain’s extreme summer temperatures. Together, these elements elevate a functional crossing into a civic asset that connects people while expressing cultural continuity, technological ambition, and Bahrain’s investment in its people and future.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2023: Competition proposal, Diyar Al Muharraq

## In print

- 2025 Oct: Insite, “Minimalism & Misinterpretations” (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2025-10-insite-minimalism-and-misinterpretations.pdf)

## Credit for publications

The Iconic Gateway, Muharraq. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-gateway/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-gateway/

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/stacked-tectonics/ -->

# Stacked Tectonics

JDT Primary School, Kozhikode. Kozhikode, India, 2012. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Stacked Tectonics is a 2,100-square-meter primary school at the JDT Islam campus in Kozhikode, extending Collaborative Architecture’s exploration of learning environments initiated with Wrap-3 in 2006. The project builds on the premise that a school’s spatial organization can shape how children experience learning, interact with others, and discover their surroundings. Rather than treating the school as a collection of classrooms connected by corridors, the design explores how architecture itself can encourage curiosity, informal exchange, and a sense of belonging. Conceived in response to a narrow site between existing campus buildings, the design transforms a spatial constraint into an architecture of playful complexity, informed by the tropical context of Kerala.

## Key facts

- Location: Kozhikode, Kerala, India
- Client: JDT Islam
- Typology: Education
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2012
- Area: 2,100 m²
- 2016 selected for the State of Architecture exhibition, Mumbai

## Classrooms as stacked volumes

The building is conceived as an assembly of distinct volumes, stacked like building blocks to create an architecture that changes with movement and perspective. This shifting composition invites children to engage with their surroundings through spatial discovery. A single-loaded corridor organizes the linear plan, while widened circulation areas become informal meeting places and stepped entrances extend learning into open-air spaces. By allowing movement, interaction, and moments of pause to become part of the school environment, the design expands the experience of learning beyond the classroom.

## A distinct identity for every classroom

Each classroom features a large window with its own shape and color, giving the space an individual identity while bringing in generous daylight and reducing reliance on artificial lighting during much of the school day. These distinctive openings reinforce the building’s playful character while helping children orient themselves within the school. The project’s emphasis on contextual resourcefulness extended to construction, which involved semi-skilled workers from the surrounding village. Stacked Tectonics won the NDTV Design & Architecture Award for Socially Relevant Design in 2014 and was selected for the *State of Architecture: Post-Independence Architecture in India* exhibition in 2016.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2012: SEED Awards, Commendation
- 2014: NDTV Design and Architecture Awards, Socially Relevant Design, Winner

## Exhibitions

- 2016: State of Architecture, post-independence architecture in India, Mumbai

## In print

- 2013 May: Society Interiors (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2013-05-society-interiors-studio-profile.pdf)

# The Legend

Skyline Builders, Kochi. Kochi, India, 2018. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Legend is a 3,800-square-foot show condominium developed for Skyline Builders in Kochi to demonstrate the potential of design-led luxury residential development in South India. Conceived around the principle that good design can strengthen commercial value, the project uses Interior Architecture as a tool to improve not only the experience of the home, but also the efficiency, desirability, and market positioning of the condominium. The layout, material language, furniture strategy, and kitchen were developed as an integrated proposition for a broad prospective market.

## Key facts

- Location: Kochi, Kerala, India
- Client: Skyline Builders
- Typology: Residential, Interior
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2018
- Area: 353 m² show condominium

## A plan made more efficient

The existing layout was comprehensively reworked to improve floor efficiency and establish a clearer functional flow. The expansive living and dining area became the spatial focus of the apartment, with the entry sequence deliberately opening toward its panoramic scale and views. Rather than relying on a highly individualized aesthetic, the interior is conceived as a calm architectural shell populated by curated furniture, allowing the apartment to feel refined while remaining accessible to a wider range of buyers.

## The kitchen that sells the home

The kitchen was treated as a critical point of both design and market value. In response to the importance of kitchen functionality and design in residential purchase decisions, the project develops a custom configuration positioned between a conventional L-shaped kitchen and an island. This hybrid arrangement combines the efficiency of a traditional work zone with the openness and social qualities of an island, making the kitchen a central component of the apartment’s contemporary luxury proposition.

## In print

- 2018 Jun: Livingetc (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2018-06-livingetc-the-legend.pdf)
- 2018 Jun: Interiors & Décor, interview issue
- 2018 Dec: Society Interiors (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2018-12-society-interiors-studio-profile.pdf)
- 2018 Dec: Indian Furniture Journal, kitchen special (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2018-11-indian-furniture-journal-kitchen-special.pdf)

## Credit for publications

The Legend, Kochi. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-legend/)

# Inverted Topography

Mezban restaurant, Kozhikode. Kozhikode, India, 2010. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Mezban reimagines a business hotel restaurant in Kozhikode as a versatile setting for dining and social exchange, transitioning from fine dining to an early-evening lounge within a restrained budget.

## Key facts

- Location: Kozhikode, Kerala, India
- Client: Hotel Asma Tower
- Typology: Hospitality
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2010
- No. 1 rated hotel in the city after relaunch
- 8 national and international awards and shortlists

## Light as the principal material

An undulating canopy of custom luminaires transforms the ceiling into an inverted topography of light. On the façade, *Thousand Moons*—a series of polished aluminum fixtures—establishes a distinctive identity and draws attention to the entrance after dark.

## A measurable change in business

The redesign demonstrated how considered spatial and lighting design can influence business performance, attracting more patrons and contributing to the hotel’s standing in the city. The project was a finalist for the Restaurant & Bar Design Awards and the SBID Awards in 2012, and was featured in [ArchDaily](https://www.archdaily.com/205233/mezban-inverted-topography-collaborative-architecture) and international publications on restaurant design.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2011: Celebration of Architecture, Winner
- 2011: Ace of Space, Hospitality, Runner-up
- 2011: IIID Design Practice of the Year, Runner-up (with Wedge-1 and Bajaj Office)
- 2012: IES Illumination Awards, Section Award
- 2012: International Design Awards (IDA), Finalist
- 2012: Restaurant & Bar Design Awards, Finalist
- 2012: SBID International Design Awards, Recreational Spaces, Finalist
- 2012: Architecture Israel, Project of the Year, Second Runner-up

## In print

- 2012 Apr: ID+C (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2012-04-id-c-inverted-topography.pdf)

# Iconic Mosque

Dubai, for Emaar. Dubai, UAE, 2018. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Collaborative Architecture’s competition proposal for a mosque in Dubai reconsiders the building’s civic and spiritual role. It challenges familiar mosque typologies while retaining the hierarchy of the prayer space, bringing a contemporary architectural expression to a place of worship, reflection and cultural exchange.

## Key facts

- Location: Dubai, United Arab Emirates
- Client: Emaar
- Typology: Religious, Civic
- Status: Competition proposal
- Year: 2018
- Consultants: Web Structures (structure); Arup (building services); Environmental Design Solutions (sustainability); Salad Dressing (landscape); BFG (façade); BSLD (lighting)
- 69 m span of the column-free dome

## A 69-meter column-free dome

A 69-meter dome spans the prayer hall, creating an expansive, column-free interior. The dome is both the project’s defining spatial gesture and a means of rethinking the mosque’s architectural form. Within this contemporary expression, the prayer space remains central.

The proposal responds to Dubai’s cultural and climatic context through the use of advanced sustainable technologies and materials.

## A destination for the city

Conceived for the faithful and visitors alike, the mosque extends its role beyond worship. It offers a setting for reflection and encounter, and gives architectural form to the project’s ambition for inclusion, tolerance and cross-cultural exchange.

## Credit for publications

Iconic Mosque, Dubai. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-mosque/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-mosque/

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/rasa-totem/ -->

# Rasa Totem

With Riyas Komu, Bengaluru. Bengaluru, India. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Conceived in collaboration with artist Riyas Komu, Rasa Totem explores the intersection of art, architecture, and India’s classical aesthetic traditions. Originally proposed as a 20-meter sculptural landmark for the new terminal at Kempegowda International Airport, Bengaluru, the project translates cultural expression into a contemporary architectural form. A scaled prototype was subsequently realized for exhibition at Index Mumbai, in collaboration with DuPont India.

## Key facts

- Location: Kempegowda International Airport, Bengaluru, India
- Client: BIAL
- Typology: Art installation
- Status: Proposal
- Prototype: Scaled prototype shown at Index Mumbai
- Collaborator: Riyas Komu
- Structure: Web Structures and Ramboll
- Prototype partners: DuPont India
- 20 m height of the proposed totem
- 8 mm high-yield steel plates

## A form drawn from classical dance

The totem’s dynamic, anthropomorphic form emerged from algorithmic studies of classical and folk dance movements in South India, particularly Karnataka. Its geometry draws on the mathematical principles underlying India’s classical art forms, while the curved central profile abstracts the facial expressions associated with the rasas—the emotional states central to Indian aesthetics.

The proposed full-scale sculpture comprises stacked, 8-millimeter-thick steel plates of varying shapes and widths, rising from a 4-meter-high, granite-clad pedestal. The scaled prototype was fabricated in 6-millimeter Corian through a collaboration with DuPont India and presented at Index Mumbai. Together, the two iterations investigate how movement, geometry, and cultural memory can converge in a sculptural landmark at the threshold of a contemporary city.

## Credit for publications

Rasa Totem, Bengaluru. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/rasa-totem/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/rasa-totem/

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/sandy-hook-memorial/ -->

# Sandy Hook Memorial

Competition entry, Newtown, Connecticut. Connecticut, USA, 2017. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Collaborative Architecture’s 2017 competition proposal for the Sandy Hook Memorial in Newtown, Connecticut, explores how architecture and landscape can create a setting for healing, introspection, and community. Conceived in response to the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, the 1,800-square-meter memorial seeks to hold individual grief within a shared civic landscape, creating spaces for gathering, remembrance, and solitary reflection. The proposal approaches the memorial as both a place of personal connection and a broader reflection on America’s relationship with gun violence.

## Key facts

- Location: Newtown, Connecticut, USA
- Client: Town of Newtown
- Typology: Memorial, Landscape
- Status: Competition entry
- Year: 2017
- Area: 1,800 m²
- Design team: Lalita Tharani, Mujib Ahmed, Prasidh, Naufan Naseer
- Consultants: Web Structures (structure); Bo Steiber Lighting Design (lighting)
- 26 chapels, one for each victim

## Chapels set into the landscape

The design preserves most of the existing landscape, introducing minimal interventions that allow the terrain to remain the memorial’s primary spatial framework. Twenty-six chapels, one for each victim, are set into the lower field, framing views and drawing the surrounding landscape into their internal courts. Sunken chapels and connecting paths maintain an understated architectural presence, allowing the experience of place to take precedence over monumental form.

Each chapel is conceived as an intimate space for families and friends to remember and reconnect. Families are invited to complete and personalize their chapel with memorabilia, while a granite bench gifted by the community provides a shared element of remembrance. Curated drawings, doodles, and anecdotes from the victims’ lives are incorporated into the concrete walls, bringing personal histories into the visitor’s journey through the memorial.

## Built with the community

Planned across three sections of the site and proposed for implementation in three phases, the memorial adopts a participatory approach to construction. Reinforced concrete forms the enclosed and semi-enclosed structures, while timber decks on mild-steel subframes and precast concrete piles support the connecting paths. The use of locally accessible construction technologies is intended to make the memorial practical to build, maintain, and, in part, realize through community participation.

Sustainability and sensitivity to the site’s fragile ecosystem underpin the proposal. Rather than imposing a singular monumental gesture, the design establishes a sequence of spaces in which landscape, material, and personal memory work together to create a place for collective remembrance.

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-souk/ -->

# The Souk

Dubai Design Week. Dubai, UAE, 2019. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Selected as the winner of Dubai Design Week’s 2019 installation program, The Souk reimagines the traditional Middle Eastern bazaar as a contemporary public realm. Three identical timber pavilions form an interconnected cluster around a shared square, creating an urban microcosm where commerce, social exchange, and collective activity shape the spatial experience.

## Key facts

- Location: Dubai, United Arab Emirates
- Client: Dubai Design Week
- Typology: Pavilion, Temporary architecture
- Status: Competition winner (unbuilt)
- Year: 2019
- Area: 125 m²
- Consultants: Web Structures (structure); Bo Steiber Lighting Design (lighting)
- 2 days planned assembly on site
- Winner Dubai Design Week 2019 installation program

## Geometry, joinery, and prefabrication

Derived from the decagon, a recurring figure in Islamic geometric patterns, the design translates a two-dimensional motif into a three-dimensional timber structure. Vertically layered decagonal elements create a dynamic spatial composition that reveals the structural, material, and expressive possibilities of architectural timber joinery. Despite its apparent complexity, the system was conceived for straightforward fabrication: the pavilion was designed for complete prefabrication and on-site assembly within two days. Although selected as the winning proposal, the installation remained unbuilt due to logistical and scheduling constraints following the competition.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2019: Dubai Design Week installation program, Winner

## In print

- 2019 Dec: Architecture + Design

- —: LinkedIn: Decoding the Pattern, The Souk, Dubai (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/decoding-pattern-souk-dubai-mujib-ahmed)

# The Spline | Stack 2

Pavilion for Concéntrico, Logroño. Logroño, Spain. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Spline | Stack 2 is Collaborative Architecture’s proposal for a public pavilion at Concéntrico, the international architecture and design festival in Logroño, Spain. It draws on the square’s intersecting pedestrian routes, translating them into a timber structure that supports public interaction while keeping views across the square open.

## Key facts

- Location: Logroño, Spain
- Client: Concéntrico, International Festival of Architecture and Design
- Typology: Pavilion, Temporary architecture
- Status: Competition entry
- 250 × 20 mm poplar strips, CNC cut and milled

## A stacked timber screen

The pavilion is formed from 250-by-20-millimeter poplar strips, CNC-cut and milled, then joined with vertical members and solid infills to create a rigid three-dimensional screen. The structure can be fabricated in smaller segments and assembled or dismantled on site, simplifying construction and logistics.

## A place to meet

A circular table around the square’s tree provides a visitor interface for information points and self-registration. The pavilion connects the square’s existing movement with a clear point of public exchange.

By combining a light-touch spatial intervention with straightforward fabrication, The Spline | Stack 2 extends the life of the square while preserving its visual openness.

## Credit for publications

The Spline | Stack 2, Logroño. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-spline/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-spline/

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/stanley-lifestyle-store/ -->

# Stanley Lifestyle Store

Anchor store for Stanley, Delhi NCR. Delhi NCR, India, 2009. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The 25,000-square-foot flagship store for Stanley brings its residential and workplace collections together within a unified retail environment. Conceived as a neutral architectural framework, the interior allows furniture, materials, color, and accessories to establish the character of each display setting. A restrained yet tactile palette maintains visual coherence across the extensive floor plate while allowing the diversity of the product range to remain central to the experience.

## Key facts

- Location: Delhi NCR, India
- Client: Stanley Lifestyles
- Typology: Retail
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2009
- Area: About 2,300 m²

## A store told as a sequence

The depth of the floor plate becomes the organizing principle of the showroom. Rather than presenting the collection as a continuous field of displays, the interior unfolds as a sequence of spatial episodes, gradually revealing different product categories as visitors move through the store. A six-meter suspended reception desk establishes a distinctive point of arrival, setting the architectural character of the space.

Screens, display units, tactile transitions, and architectonic envelopes define the sequence, creating distinct settings without fragmenting the overall environment. These elements operate simultaneously as spatial dividers and display frameworks, establishing visual relationships between individual collections while maintaining continuity across the showroom.

## Reimagining the retail interface

The project became an opportunity to challenge the conventional relationship between retail architecture and product display. The studio pushed the client to reconsider the store as more than a backdrop for merchandise, advocating a more radical and architecturally experiential approach to the retail interface. This dialogue between commercial objectives and spatial experimentation extended the brief beyond the immediate requirements of the showroom.

It was through this design exercise that Wedge-1 emerged—an independent design exploration that carried the inquiry into a more radical architectural expression. Subsequently widely published internationally and recognized through multiple awards and international shortlistings, Wedge-1 demonstrates how a commercially driven interior project can become a catalyst for broader design investigation.

## Architecture as a frame for experience

The Stanley showroom treats retail architecture as an active instrument of presentation rather than an object competing for attention. Its role is to establish the conditions in which products can be experienced in relation to one another, allowing variations in material, color, scale, and use to become legible. More significantly, the project illustrates Collaborative Architecture’s approach to design as an iterative process of inquiry: engaging with a client’s commercial brief while identifying opportunities to extend its architectural and experiential ambition.

## In print

- 2012 Apr: Design Today (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2012-04-design-today-wedge-1-and-stanley-delhi.pdf)
- 2013 May: Society Interiors, profile (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2013-05-society-interiors-studio-profile.pdf)

## Credit for publications

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/national-unity-pavilion/ -->

# National Unity Pavilion

Notions of India. India, India, 2021. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The National Unity Pavilion is Collaborative Architecture’s winning proposal for Notions of India, an international competition organized by Tata Steel to commemorate 75 years of Indian independence. Selected as one of three winning entries from 575 submissions, the project asks a fundamental question: can architecture give spatial form to the idea of a nation shaped by multiple histories, cultures, beliefs, and languages?

The pavilion forms part of Collaborative Architecture’s broader inquiry into Architecture That Fosters Democracy—a body of speculative architectural work exploring how space can enable deliberation, plurality, civic participation, and non-violence. Alongside the studio’s Peace Pavilion, conceived for a national war memorial competition, it investigates architecture not simply as a representation of collective ideals, but as a framework within which those ideals can be encountered, negotiated, and contested.

Rather than reducing India to a singular architectural symbol, the National Unity Pavilion constructs its identity through overlapping cultural, philosophical, and democratic references. It interprets the nation as a living palimpsest: an evolving collective consciousness grounded in historical memory, constitutional values, and the ideal of unity in diversity. In doing so, the project considers democracy not as a settled condition or an aspiration to uniformity, but as an ongoing negotiation between difference and belonging.

## Key facts

- Location: India
- Organizer: Tata Steel
- Typology: Pavilion, Civic
- Status: One of the three winning entries, international competition
- Year: 2021
- Structure: Web Structures, Ramboll
- Video: Link to be supplied
- 75 years of independence commemorated

## Democracy as the coexistence of difference

Situated within India’s heterogeneous social and cultural fabric, the pavilion explores how architecture might accommodate divergent identities within a shared civic framework. Its conceptual foundations draw on the philosophical lineage of the Buddha, Ashoka, and Gandhi, bringing traditions of non-violence and ethical coexistence into dialogue with the democratic principles of the Constitution. Federalism, pluralism, and the freedom to differ inform an architectural proposition that resists a single, authoritative interpretation of nationhood.

The project does not seek to resolve India’s cultural complexity into a unified visual language. Instead, it gives form to the relationship between distinct parts and a collective whole. The pavilion becomes a setting in which visitors can encounter the idea of India as a continuing civic project—one shaped by its many communities, histories, contradictions, and aspirations. Unity is understood not as the absence of difference, but as the capacity to sustain difference through shared principles and mutual recognition.

## A stupa, a mandala, and a civic landscape

The pavilion’s overall diameter and volume draw from the Great Stupa at Sanchi, translating the scale and symbolic resonance of an ancient architectural form into a contemporary civic setting. Its geometry is organized through overlapping mandalas, establishing the spatial order and sequence of the pavilion. A circular route guides visitors through the experience, evoking the Dharma Chakra and its resonances across India’s major religious and philosophical traditions.

Encircling the pavilion, a series of pylons represents India’s states and union territories. Set within a reflecting pool, they establish a collective perimeter around the central space while expressing the relationship between regional identities and the larger union. Each pylon also serves as an entry point into a wider cultural narrative, connected to a QR-coded disc embedded in the circular gallery floor. Through digital interfaces, visitors can access additional media, extending the physical experience into a broader exploration of India’s regional and cultural plurality.

At the center of the composition, an amphitheater gathers around a Bodhi tree, conceived as the genius loci—the spirit and living center of the place. The tree anchors a shared civic space for encounter, dialogue, and collective reflection. Here, visitors can exchange ideas, deliberate differences, and participate in a common setting without the expectation of uniformity. The architecture brings together the philosophical resonance of an ancient landscape and the contemporary democratic imperative to make room for discussion, critique, and solidarity.

## From national symbol to democratic practice

The National Unity Pavilion extends Collaborative Architecture’s exploration of the relationship between architecture and democratic life. Its companion project, the Peace Pavilion, approaches this question through a different institutional and spatial premise: conceived at the entrance to a national war museum, it repositions peace as the primary curatorial narrative, transforming the threshold into a public plaza and contemplative forum. Where the Peace Pavilion questions the conventional glorification of conflict, the National Unity Pavilion examines the conditions through which a plural society might recognize and sustain its collective identity.

Together, these projects form part of a continuing investigation into *Architecture That Fosters Democracy*. They draw on culturally embedded spatial practices and historical allegories rather than reproducing established democratic archetypes. Their ambition is to create settings for public encounter in which plurality, deliberation, and non-violence become spatial and social propositions.

Yet the projects also acknowledge the limits of architecture’s agency. A pavilion cannot, by itself, secure democratic participation or resolve political and cultural differences. Its role is more provisional and critical: to establish conditions in which people can gather, reflect, disagree, and imagine forms of coexistence. The National Unity Pavilion therefore moves beyond the representation of national identity to consider architecture as a medium through which the possibilities—and contradictions—of democracy can be experienced and continually renegotiated.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2021: Notions of India, international competition, Tata Steel, winning entry

## In print

- 2025 Oct: Insite, “Minimalism & Misinterpretations” (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/features/2025-10-insite-minimalism-and-misinterpretations.pdf)

## Online

# Urnes Stave Heritage Center

Urnesløven Gavl, Norway. Norway, Norway. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Developed for an international competition, the Urnes Stave Heritage Center proposes a contemporary visitor experience rooted in Nordic timber traditions and regional craftsmanship. Located on a sloping site between two roads near the UNESCO-listed Urnes Stave Church in Norway, the three-level scheme uses the terrain to organize its program while establishing a restrained architectural presence within the historic landscape. The proposal interprets vernacular building traditions through abstraction rather than imitation, connecting contemporary construction with the region’s cultural and material heritage.

## Key facts

- Location: Urnes, Luster, Norway
- Client: International competition, Institute of Norwegian Architects
- Typology: Museum, Heritage center
- Status: Competition entry
- Structure: Web Structures, Singapore
- 3 levels set into the slope
- CLT timber superstructure on a concrete base

## A quiet form in dark timber

The brief called for a building that would not compete with its historic setting. Drawing on the tectonics and character of the region’s timber architecture, the design develops an abstracted roof profile that follows the contours of the hillside while opening views of the fjord from different levels. Partially submerged into the terrain, the building minimizes its apparent mass, while smoked, dark-stained timber cladding establishes a visual relationship with the historic church.

## Rooted in local life

The landscape is conceived as an extension of the visitor experience, with areas dedicated to local produce and agriculture. These productive landscapes offer an experiential introduction to the region while creating opportunities for local community engagement and reinforcing the project’s sustainability objectives.

The proposed structure combines reinforced concrete for the below-ground portions with cross-laminated timber (CLT) for the superstructure. This hybrid construction strategy draws on timber’s structural and environmental performance while placing contemporary building technology within a longstanding Nordic tradition of material craft. The result is an architecture intended to remain understated in the landscape while connecting heritage, local life, and contemporary construction.

## Awards and shortlists

- —: Urnes Stave Church heritage center, international competition, results awaited

## Credit for publications

# Wedge-1

Stanley, Mumbai. Mumbai, India, 2009. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Wedge-1 is a full-scale prototype for a freestanding luxury retail building for Stanley Lifestyles. Built for an exhibition in Mumbai, it tested how spatial form, product display and visitor movement could shape a more experiential retail environment. The experiment became a precursor to the Stanley Lifestyle Showroom.

## Key facts

- Location: Mumbai, India
- Client: Stanley Lifestyles
- Typology: Retail, Prototype
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2009
- Area: 300 m²
- Lighting design: Collaborative Architecture
- 5 awards and international shortlists

## A box stretched, cut and folded

The design transforms a simple rectangular volume into a pinwheel of trapezoidal spaces arranged around a central gathering area. Openings in the perimeter wall alternately reveal and conceal the displays, drawing visitors inward. Above, 1,200-millimeter T5 lamps set at shifting angles form a canopy of light that completes the interior.

## From prototype to recognition

Wedge-1 allowed the studio to explore how retail could be conceived as an architectural experience, rather than a sequence of displays. The project won Project of the Year at Architecture Israel in 2012 and was a finalist in the 2011 FX International Interior Design Awards. It was also published internationally, including by [ArchDaily](https://www.archdaily.com/94905/wedge-1-collaborative-architecture).

The project demonstrates how a focused design experiment can inform a larger retail concept, connecting spatial organization, display and visitor experience.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2010: Ace of Space, Runner-up
- 2011: FX International Interior Design Awards, Finalist
- 2011: IIID Design Practice of the Year, Runner-up

# Wrap-4

KTC Hyundai Showroom, Kerala. Kerala, India, 2007. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Wrap-4 transforms a 1,100-square-meter former warehouse into a Hyundai showroom for the KTC Group, reinterpreting the conventional typology of automobile retail. Set directly along the city’s main street, the building offers an uninterrupted 60-meter frontage that becomes the primary instrument of the architectural intervention. Rather than treating the vehicle display as an arrangement of cars within a retail floor, the studio reverses the brief, positioning the display itself as the organizing principle of the space. The result is an architectural environment in which product, space, and street converge within a singular, continuous gesture.

## Key facts

- Location: Kerala, India
- Client: KTC Group
- Typology: Retail, Showroom
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2007
- Area: 1,100 m² warehouse
- 60 m uninterrupted street frontage
- 4 awards, including the Bienal Miami

## The display as urban spectacle

A continuous architectural wrap merges floor, walls, and ceiling into a unified spatial surface, incorporating the vehicles into the larger composition. The intervention establishes a visual connection between the showroom interior and the movement of traffic and pedestrians beyond its frontage. Conceived as a 60-meter urban billboard, the façade translates the kinetic character of the street into an architectural expression, transforming the conventional car showroom into a public-facing display. The vehicles become integral to the spatial narrative rather than objects placed within a neutral backdrop.

## Curves that define spatial hierarchy

A sinuous, sinusoidal partition establishes a subtle boundary between the public showroom and the more private lounge areas, introducing spatial distinction without compromising the continuity of the larger volume. This formal language extends to the spiral staircase, whose custom-fabricated, three-dimensionally profiled cantilevered steps demonstrate a considered integration of geometry, engineering, and craftsmanship. Together, these elements accommodate Hyundai’s comprehensive retail and service program while maintaining a coherent architectural identity.

Wrap-4 received a First Honorable Mention at the 2007 Bienal Miami.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2007: Bienal Miami, First Honorable Mention
- 2007: A+D Spectrum Innovative Interior Award, Commendation
- 2007: IIID Awards, Retail Spaces, Winner
- 2007: Better Interiors Innovation Award, Retail Spaces, Winner

# Project Alpha

ICON Initiative 99, Texas. Texas, USA, 2025. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Project Alpha is Collaborative Architecture’s proposal for Initiative 99, ICON’s global challenge exploring the potential of 3D-printed housing to address affordability. The project questions the premise that housing affordability is primarily an engineering problem, solvable through cheaper materials and faster construction. While additive manufacturing can reduce the cost of erecting a dwelling, the proposal argues that the cost of a dwelling is not the cost of housing. True affordability depends on a broader framework of land economics, finance, regulation, equitable access, and policies that protect communities from displacement.

## Key facts

- Location: Texas, United States
- Client: ICON, Initiative 99
- Typology: Housing, Research
- Status: Competition proposal
- Year: 2025
- Area: Single unit 428 sq ft, twin unit 851 sq ft (built-up)
- Budget: US$100,000 per dwelling, set by the challenge
- 48 dwellings in the community plan

## Two curved walls, an adaptable spatial system

The proposal prioritizes a familiar housing form over an expression of the printer’s formal capabilities, seeking social acceptance across diverse communities. Its fundamental unit is organized around two curved walls that taper toward their free ends, creating a flexible spatial framework for living, sleeping, and other domestic functions. The geometry allows units to be reconfigured and combined, generating varied interior arrangements and clusters organized around shared public spaces.

Bedrooms and living areas are arranged diagonally to allow the unit to respond to the sun path and specific site conditions. A complementary twin-unit configuration expands the spatial vocabulary, enabling larger homes and collective arrangements without requiring an entirely new design for every variation. Adaptability and repeatability are central to the proposal, supporting deployment across different communities and contexts.

## Built for a long life in a demanding climate

The proposed roof combines glulam and cross-laminated timber with insulated metal roofing and a timber-board soffit. This assembly is intended to support thermal comfort while reducing on-site work and cost variability during large-scale deployment. Radiant floors provide heating and cooling for the seasonal conditions of Texas, while recycled or sustainably sourced wood and cast terrazzo are proposed as flooring finishes. The environmental strategy also includes ENERGY STAR-rated appliances, low-VOC finishes, and LED lighting powered by solar energy.

## Affordability as a condition, not a milestone

Project Alpha recognizes a fundamental paradox of successful development: improvements in design and place-making can accelerate gentrification, displacing the very communities they are intended to benefit. The proposal therefore situates technological innovation within a broader framework of policy safeguards designed to protect long-term affordability.

Potential mechanisms include community land trusts, shared-equity ownership, resale covenants, land-value capture, and zoning reform. These instruments seek to preserve the affordability gains enabled by efficient construction and prevent them from being eroded by speculative land markets. Project Alpha positions 3D printing not as a standalone solution, but as one component of a comprehensive housing strategy—one that integrates construction technology, spatial quality, equitable access, and lasting affordability.

## Writing

- 2026 Jan: The Collaborative Logs: Reflections 2026, are we serving right? (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/reflections-2026-we-serving-right-mujib-ahmed-noojf)

## Credit for publications

# 50th Cross Road

Show apartment, PVS Developers, Kerala. Kerala, India, 2020. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Designed as a show apartment for PVS Developers in Kozhikode, 50th Cross Road supported the developer’s repositioning into the luxury condominium market. Conceived as an aspirational living environment, the 204-square-meter, three-bedroom residence demonstrates how considered Interior Architecture, material selection, and specification can elevate a residential offering while remaining aligned with the broader project standards. Collaborative Architecture’s scope extended beyond the apartment’s interiors to establish the project’s overall material palette, tonal direction, and specification framework.

## Key facts

- Location: Kerala, India
- Client: PVS Developers
- Typology: Residential, Interior
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2020
- Area: 204 m², three bedrooms

## A shell for curated pieces

The apartment responds to the aesthetic expectations of the developer’s intended buyers through a rich, tactile material palette, with wood as its defining element. Rather than imposing a highly personalized design language, the interior is conceived as a restrained architectural shell, animated by carefully curated furnishings and objects. This approach creates an aspirational yet broadly accessible residential experience, allowing prospective buyers to imagine the space as their own.

The bathrooms were designed as repeatable typologies for deployment across the wider development. Through precise detailing and a considered material palette, standardized specifications become an instrument of design quality, elevating the everyday experience while maintaining consistency and commercial viability. The project demonstrates how a coherent specification strategy can support brand repositioning and establish a distinctive proposition within the affordable luxury segment.
