# Material Cartographies

1 × 1 · Bahrain Pavilion, Venice Biennale 2027. Venice, Italy, 2026. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

1 × 1 is Collaborative Architecture’s proposal for the Bahrain Pavilion at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale, investigating the material dependencies of contemporary architecture through the lens of a single square meter of built space. Titled The Material Cartography of the Built Space of Bahrain, the project shifts architectural inquiry from the scale of the skyline to the origins, journeys, and environmental costs of the materials that constitute the built environment.

Architecture has to respond to two opposing, increasingly contradictory conditions of its own existence—two divergent epistemologies through which the built environment is understood. The first is rooted in the *phenomenological*: architecture as an embodied experience of place, shaped by perception, memory, material presence, climate, culture, and the human relationship with space. The second is revealed through *material cartography and trajectories*: architecture understood as the outcome of extended networks of extraction, manufacture, energy, transportation, labor, and exchange that frequently transcend the very places in which buildings stand.

These two conditions are increasingly difficult to reconcile. Architecture is experienced locally, yet produced through global systems; it is perceived as a coherent presence in a particular place, yet materially constituted by resources and processes dispersed across distant territories. The phenomenological experience of architecture may suggest rootedness and permanence, while its material genealogy reveals dependencies, environmental consequences, and geopolitical vulnerabilities that remain largely invisible to its occupants. 1 × 1 brings these divergent readings into a single field of inquiry, asking how architecture can remain meaningfully rooted in place while acknowledging the extensive material networks that make its existence possible.

A single square meter of a Bahraini house weighs approximately 1,219 kilograms. Its constituent materials may originate thousands of kilometers away, pass through multiple stages of extraction, processing, and transportation, and converge at a building site seemingly detached from their geological and industrial origins. By tracing these trajectories, the pavilion reveals architecture as a territorial network shaped by resource availability, energy systems, trade routes, and geopolitical vulnerabilities.

The project extends Collaborative Architecture’s research into material scarcity, circularity, and the systems of production that shape contemporary architecture. It challenges the assumption that architecture’s relationship with place can be understood through its physical presence alone, proposing instead that this relationship must also be examined through material knowledge, environmental responsibility, and an understanding of the resources on which buildings depend.

## Key facts

- Location: Bahrain Pavilion, Biennale Architettura, Venice
- Client: Kingdom of Bahrain, national participation, Venice Biennale 2027
- Typology: Exhibition, Research
- Status: Competition proposal
- Year: 2026
- Research: Collaborative Lab
- 1,219 kg of material in one square meter of a Bahraini home, the reference assembly
- ≈16,300 km longest trajectory: iron ore from Minas Gerais, Brazil
- ≈70% of the material energy enters the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz

## Architecture is located not where it is built

Almost none of the principal raw materials in a square meter of Bahraini construction originate entirely within Bahrain. The research traces the material pedigree of reinforcing steel, aluminum, cement, crushed gabbro, sand, and flat glass, following each from extraction and processing to its arrival at the building site. The investigation records material origins, transportation routes and modes, distances traveled, freight requirements, processing energy, embodied carbon, and opportunities for recycled feedstock.

Bahrain presents a particularly revealing case of *material inversion.* It imports much of the raw material used in construction, has manufactured substantial areas of its own land, and exports a significant portion of its energy in the form of aluminum, very little of which enters its domestic construction sector. The conventional relationship between place, material, and architecture is therefore inverted: the physical presence of a building does not necessarily reveal the territories, industries, and resources on which it depends.

The resulting cartography situates the Bahraini built environment within a wider regional and global system. It exposes the concentration of supply routes, the dependencies created by long-distance material flows, and the environmental implications of a construction economy reliant on imported resources. As material scarcity, rising sea levels, and geopolitical instability intensify, these dependencies become questions of resilience as much as sustainability.

## Trajectories of a square meter

The exhibition makes these otherwise invisible supply chains spatially legible. Material trajectories converge from distant geological and industrial territories, linking extraction sites, processing centers, ports, and transport corridors to a single square meter of construction. The gallery floor becomes a map at a scale of one meter to 1,200 kilometers, transforming the exhibition into an immersive representation of the geography embedded within the built environment.

High-strength steel ribbons, 25 millimeters high, trace the principal material routes across the floor, walls, and roof, recalling the iconography of oceanic movement. Their form reflects the dependence of Bahrain’s construction economy on maritime transport, with approximately 95 percent of the materials in the study transported by sea. A glazed opening in the floor represents the Strait of Hormuz, while shifting LED strips register changing levels of supply-chain vulnerability.

At an interactive console, visitors can compose their own square meter of construction and observe how material choices affect transportation distances, energy requirements, and carbon emissions. The research reveals counterintuitive relationships: aluminum, despite representing a small proportion of the material mass, can account for a disproportionately large share of upfront embodied carbon. It also demonstrates that material impacts must be considered within the wider life cycle of a building, where retention of existing structures and the demand for mechanical cooling can have consequences beyond the initial choice of construction materials.

## Making and scarcity

The pavilion is conceived as a constructed research instrument rather than a display that merely illustrates its findings. Visitors encounter the research through physical specimens, spatial relationships, and interactive tools, connecting the abstract systems of global production to the tangible substance of architecture.

At the center of the exhibition, two full-scale specimens of one square meter are placed in direct comparison: one representing contemporary construction and the other vernacular building using coral stone. Their material composition, resource dependencies, energy implications, and carbon attributes establish a comparative framework for examining different modes of construction.

The comparison brings the project’s two epistemologies into direct relation. The phenomenological dimension invites consideration of how architecture is experienced through material presence, climate, cultural memory, and the specificities of place. The cartographic dimension asks what lies beyond that immediate experience: where the materials originate, what resources they consume, which territories they connect, and what environmental costs they carry. Neither perspective is sufficient in isolation. Together, they enable a more complete understanding of architecture as both a lived environment and a material condition embedded within larger ecological and economic systems.

The comparison opens a broader inquiry into the intelligence embedded in vernacular building, the potential of new materials and processes, and the environmental value of retaining and adapting existing structures. Scarcity is approached not simply as a limitation to be overcome through substitution, but as a condition that demands more informed decisions about what is extracted, what is imported, what is built, and what is preserved.

## From material research to national design policy

1 × 1 is conceived as the beginning of a research undertaking extending beyond the Biennale. The installation serves as a working prototype for a public Material Mapping Registry, intended to consolidate evidence on the origins, environmental impacts, and dependencies of the materials that constitute Bahrain’s built environment.

Developed as a foundation for engagement with government agencies, including those concerned with industry, the proposed registry could inform built-environment and industrial policy, support a comprehensive framework for adaptive reuse, and contribute to the formulation of a National Design Policy for Bahrain. The ambition is to translate architectural research into a practical instrument for decision-making—connecting material intelligence with resource resilience, industrial strategy, and the long-term performance of the built environment.

Through 1 × 1, Collaborative Architecture positions the square meter as both a unit of measurement and a unit of responsibility. By tracing the material origins of architecture, the project asks how a nation can build with greater awareness of its environmental limits, industrial dependencies, and inherited resources. It reframes material cartography as a means of understanding place—not only through where architecture stands or how it is experienced, but through the networks, decisions, and ecological consequences that make its construction possible.

## Writing

- 2026 Oct: The Collaborative Logs: Architecture is Located NOT Where it is Built (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/architecture-located-where-built-mujib-ahmed-ki4rc)

## Credit for publications

# The Measured City

National Pavilion of the UAE, Venice Biennale 2027. Venice, Italy, 2026. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Measured City is Collaborative Architecture’s proposal for the UAE National Pavilion at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale, positioning the United Arab Emirates as a living laboratory for urban futures in arid regions. Moving beyond the spectacle of iconic skylines, the project employs data-driven inquiry to reveal the underlying systems, environmental forces, and spatial dynamics shaping the country’s urban evolution. Through the critical mapping of decades of urban development, the pavilion examines how the Emirates have transformed their environments, negotiated global and local influences, and established new models of urban habitation.

## Key facts

- Location: National Pavilion of the United Arab Emirates, Arsenale, Venice
- Client: National Pavilion UAE, Biennale Architettura 2027
- Typology: Exhibition, Research
- Status: Competition proposal
- Year: 2026
- Collaborators: Dr. Shibu Raman, Dr. Filippo Osella
- 14 indices mapped, from health and education to biodiversity, governance and industry

## Beyond the iconic skyline | Hidden cartographies: past, present, future

Earlier pavilion narratives have drawn attention to the perils of speculative urbanism and the consequences of rapid urban transformation. The Measured City takes a complementary, deliberately contrarian approach: rather than treating the UAE primarily through the imagery of its architecture, it investigates the accumulated evidence of its urbanization. It brings together historical and contemporary datasets from across the Emirates to identify shared trajectories, distinctive regional characteristics, emerging patterns, and areas requiring further intervention.

The proposition is to understand the city not as a static composition of buildings and infrastructure, but as a dynamic system shaped by demographic change, public policy, economic activity, ecological transformation, and cultural exchange. The resulting cartographies reveal both the achievements and the shortcomings of urban development, establishing a basis for informed debate and future research.

The pavilion invites its audience to look beyond the familiar representations of the UAE as a collection of spectacular skylines. Instead, it presents the country as an intricately measured living system—one whose urban futures can be understood through the relationships between data, territory, human experience, and the environment.

## Fourteen indices, overlaid

At the heart of the project is a multilayered cultural, ecological, and spatial atlas assembled through the systematic analysis of current and archived government datasets. Fourteen interconnected indices provide a framework for examining the social, economic, environmental, and institutional dimensions of urban change. These include population and demographic shifts, health, education, employment, consumption, social and cultural infrastructure, food security, patents and regionally developed systems, biodiversity lost and restored, the water–land interface, governance and policy, sustainability measures, and industrial development.

Rather than presenting these indicators in isolation, the pavilion overlays them to expose relationships that conventional statistical reporting can obscure. The interaction between population growth and infrastructure, consumption and resource security, urban expansion and biodiversity, or policy commitments and measurable environmental outcomes can reveal where systems reinforce one another, where tensions emerge, and where targeted design or policy interventions may have the greatest effect.

This approach extends beyond the collection of statistics. It translates large and complex datasets into legible visual narratives, enabling visitors to recognize patterns across different Emirates and across successive periods of urban development. The maps and visualizations become instruments of critical inquiry: documenting progress, questioning assumptions, and identifying opportunities for more resilient and contextually responsive urban futures.

## Hybrid urbanism | Global systems, local cultures

The UAE offers a distinctive context in which to examine the relationship between globally networked urbanism and deeply rooted cultural patterns. Its cities bring together international capital, technologies, labor, infrastructure, and architectural practices within environments shaped by aridity, water scarcity, climatic extremes, and particular cultural histories.

The pavilion investigates the consequences of this convergence. How does the blending of global architectural languages with local patterns of inhabitation transform urban identity? How do infrastructure, public space, social and cultural institutions, and environmental systems mediate the relationship between cosmopolitan ambition and cultural continuity? And what can measurable evidence reveal about the long-term performance of these hybrid urban conditions?

By mapping these relationships, The Measured City seeks to move beyond a binary reading of globalized development as either an achievement or a liability. It examines the specific outcomes of the UAE’s urban evolution, asking where its adaptive strategies have succeeded, where contradictions remain, and how the lessons embedded in its experience might inform other rapidly urbanizing regions.

## A white box of vaults

The exhibition architecture establishes a deliberately restrained setting for the complexity of the research. Conceived as a white-box gallery, the installation draws on architectural traditions of the UAE and the wider region while responding to the heritage character of the Biennale venue. A sequence of self-supporting vaults, constructed from 40-millimeter plywood frameworks with mild-steel bracing and gypsum-board cladding, creates a series of compact, interconnected galleries.

The vaulted forms provide more than a neutral container for information. They establish a spatial rhythm through which the visitor encounters the research, balancing the continuity of the exhibition with the distinct character of individual displays. Their material economy and restrained finish allow the cartographic content to remain central, while giving the exhibition a clear architectural identity.

The gallery surfaces become an active interface between architecture and data. Maps, diagrams, infographics, interactive displays, physical and three-dimensional data representations, prototypes, and digital projections communicate the research at different scales and levels of engagement. A defined visitor route connects these individual spaces into a cumulative experience, allowing each gallery to function both as an information environment and as an architectural space in its own right.

The exhibition thus translates abstract datasets into a spatial sequence. Visitors move through the evidence of urban transformation rather than encountering it solely as a collection of charts or screens. Architecture becomes the medium through which the relationships between territory, data, and urban experience are made perceptible.

## From measurement to urban futures

The Measured City is conceived not merely as a retrospective account of the UAE’s urban development, but as a framework for evaluating its future. By assembling data across time, geography, and policy domains, the project creates opportunities to identify effective practices, expose persistent vulnerabilities, and examine the implications of current development trajectories.

Its relevance extends beyond the Emirates. Rapidly urbanizing regions across arid and climatically vulnerable territories face related questions concerning resource security, ecological resilience, infrastructure, social cohesion, and the relationship between global ambition and local identity. The UAE’s experience provides a valuable field of investigation—not as a universal model to be replicated, but as a body of evidence from which other regions can draw context-specific lessons while recognizing approaches that may warrant caution.

Through The Measured City, Collaborative Architecture positions data as an instrument of architectural and urban inquiry. The project proposes that a deeper understanding of cities emerges when their visible forms are read alongside the systems that produce them, the populations that inhabit them, and the environmental conditions that sustain them. By making these hidden relationships legible, the pavilion seeks to inform a more critically grounded, ecologically responsive, and culturally continuous approach to the urban futures of the UAE and the wider arid world.

## Credit for publications

The Measured City, Venice. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-measured-city/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-measured-city/

# BGRT Mumbai

R&D campus, Navi Mumbai. Navi Mumbai, India. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Commissioned by the Bearys Group, BGRT Mumbai is a 40,000-square-meter campus for general and pharmaceutical research. Building on the group’s Bengaluru campus, home to Reflected Topography, the proposal retains the masterplan’s footprint while reworking its architectural expression through a climate-responsive façade strategy. The project targets LEED Platinum certification.

## Key facts

- Location: Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
- Client: Bearys Group
- Typology: Research campus, Workplace
- Status: Detailed design
- Area: About 40,000 m²
- Certification: LEED Platinum, targeted
- West façade with mechanized Accoya louvers

## A linear campus, brought together

The masterplan’s fragmented linear superblock is unified by a continuous, rhythmic façade that emphasizes the campus’s length and panoramic outlook. Stepped mini-atriums connect the separate blocks, giving the campus a shared architectural identity.

## A façade calibrated to the sun

Facing west, the main façade is exposed to strong afternoon sun. Mechanized bi-fold louvers in Accoya timber are paired with thermally insulated solid panels clad in custom glass-fiber-reinforced concrete. The fins are positioned in response to the sun path; an upgraded system could allow them to tilt mechanically with seasonal changes.

The proposal brings the studio’s contextual and environmentally responsive approach to a research campus, aligning its architectural character with the site, the masterplan and the demands of the climate.

## Credit for publications

BGRT Mumbai, Navi Mumbai. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/bgrt-mumbai/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/bgrt-mumbai/

# Bearys Wafira

Residences, Dubai Healthcare City. Dubai, UAE. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

In Dubai Healthcare City, Bearys Wafira is conceived as a limited-edition residence where sophisticated luxury is shaped by its arid setting. Collaborative Architecture’s interior design spans the grand lobby, club floors, four condominiums and penthouse, bringing together a human-centered approach, considered detailing and a refined palette of bespoke finishes.

Bearys Wafira is due for completion in 2029. More details will follow.

## Key facts

- Location: Dubai Healthcare City, Dubai, United Arab Emirates
- Client: Bearys Global
- Typology: Residential, Interior
- Scope: Grand lobby, club floors, four condominiums and penthouse
- Status: Under construction, due for completion in 2029
- Architect: NMS, Calicut
- Resident architect: Arif & Bintoak, Dubai
- Consultants: LET, Dubai (lighting design); SEED, Dubai (building services); Fencon (façade); Excom, Dubai (cost); ARSA, India (structure); Acoustic Logic LLC, Dubai (acoustics)
- 4 condominiums and a penthouse
- Universal access, part of the design approach

## Bespoke interiors

Custom-developed finishes and a bespoke kitchen give the residences a distinct material character. Carefully resolved details carry this language across the interiors, balancing precision and refinement with the everyday experience of living.

## Spaces for living together

Public and communal areas are designed to encourage encounter and support a connected residential community. From the lobby to the club floors, shared spaces give social life a central place in the project.

## Integrated systems

The project combines design and material innovation with advanced systems for lighting, automation, water and solid-waste management, alongside biometric, IT and communication infrastructure. Universal access is also part of the design approach.

Wafira brings sophisticated residential design into dialogue with environmental performance, bespoke craftsmanship and the experience of space.

# MillerKnoll Experience Center

Experience center, Bengaluru. Bengaluru, India, 2025. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The MillerKnoll Experience Center brings together the brand’s strategic ambitions with the demands of retail and daily operation. Collaborative Architecture transformed a challenging interior—its low ceilings, deep structural beams and exposed services—into an immersive setting for experiencing the collection, making the center both a brand environment and a retail interface.

## Key facts

- Location: Bengaluru, India
- Client: Bearys Innomark for MillerKnoll
- Typology: Experience center, Retail
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2025
- Performance: India’s first Net Zero retail space, and one of the three best MillerKnoll experience centers worldwide
- 1st Net Zero retail space in India
- Top 3 MillerKnoll experience centers worldwide

## Design through reference, not imitation

The interior draws on the legacy of the designers associated with MillerKnoll and their influence on modernism. Rather than reproduce familiar forms, the design translates their spirit of experimentation into new architectural elements. The chair display system explores the material logic of bent plywood, with references to the Eames Case Study House; the floating staircase draws on the sculptural language of Warren Platner’s Lounge series.

## Turning constraints into experience

A considered response to the existing structure makes its limitations part of the design. Natural light, available through much of the day, supports the experience of the space, while display and circulation bring the collection into focus.

The completed center is described in the project brief as India’s first Net Zero retail space and MillerKnoll’s first Net Zero interface globally. It reflects the studio’s integrated approach: translating brand identity, spatial constraints and environmental ambition into a coherent experience.

# Wrap-3

Computer learning center for an orphanage, Kozhikode. Kozhikode, India, 2006. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Completed in 2006, Wrap-3 is a first-generation computer training center for an orphanage in South India. Designed for primary and secondary school students, the space takes the child’s perception as its point of departure, shaping an informal learning environment that feels familiar and inviting.

## Key facts

- Location: Kozhikode, Kerala, India
- Client: JDT Islam
- Typology: Education, Interior
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2006
- 2010 Aga Khan Award for Architecture, first-round nomination
- 2010 SKETCH exhibition curated by Tadao Ando, Mexico

## Layers of color and light

The interior is conceived as a series of wraps, juxtaposed to create overlapping layers of color and space. Natural light streaming from outside animates these layers, producing shifting views and spatial impressions.

## A space for discovery

Childlike, doodle-inspired cut-outs punctuate the wraps. They function as graphic marks and as integral architectural elements, encouraging curiosity and accidental discovery. Together, the layered surfaces, openings and changing light create what the project describes as a “spatial kaleidoscope.”

Wrap-3’s ideas later informed Stacked Tectonics, a 1,858-square-meter school building by the studio on the same campus, extending the project’s exploration of child-centered space to a larger scale.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2006: IIID Award, Spaces of Social Relevance, Winner
- 2006: A+D Spectrum Innovative Interior Award, Honorable Mention
- 2008: DesignShare, Educational Spaces, Recognized Value Award
- 2010: Aga Khan Award for Architecture, first-round nomination

## Exhibitions

- 2010: SKETCH, curated by Tadao Ando, Universidad de Monterrey, Mexico, with d3

## In print

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/prototype-non/ -->

# Prototype N[ON]

Retail concept for Moroso, Mumbai. Mumbai, India, 2008. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

Temporary architecture serves as a testing ground for ideas that inform the evolving body of work at Collaborative Architecture. Conceived as spatial experiments, these prototypes provide a framework for testing, refining and reconfiguring architectural propositions before their translation into larger-scale applications. Prototype N[ON] is an early manifestation of this research-driven approach, establishing a lineage of experimental constructs that continues to inform the studio’s practice.

Presented as part of a design showcase organized by Universal Expo and Index Media at their 2008 trade exhibition in Mumbai, India, the project brought together ten prominent architectural practices, each invited to develop a conceptual and spatial intervention within a 5 × 5-meter footprint.

Conceived as a prototypical retail interface for the Italian furniture brand Moroso, Prototype N[ON] explored the possibilities of retail space as an evolving spatial construct. Rather than approaching the brief as a conventional display environment, the project used the pavilion as a testing ground for alternative spatial strategies, examining how a limited footprint could accommodate new relationships between enclosure, display and spatial experience.

## Key facts

- Location: Mumbai, India
- Client: Index Fairs, for Moroso
- Typology: Retail, Exhibition, Temporary architecture
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2008
- Area: 5 × 5 m

## Material Logic and Construction

The project’s material and construction logic reinforces its experimental premise. The tectonic elements are weaved to create the space. Simple MDF panels, supported by mild-steel frameworks, were prefabricated and assembled on site, with an acrylic emulsion finish unifying the assembly. The resulting system demonstrates how a deliberately restrained palette of materials and straightforward construction techniques can support an exploratory architectural proposition.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2008: IIID Awards, Design Practice of the Year, Winner
- 2009: A+D Spectrum Innovative Interior Award, Commendation

## In print

- 2009 Jul: Buildotech

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/tree-of-life/ -->

# Tree of Life

Shoah Memorial competition entry, Lyon. Lyon, France, 2023. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Shoah Memorial in Lyon is conceived as a place of remembrance for the Jewish victims of the Holocaust and a setting for collective reflection on one of the darkest chapters in human history. Beyond commemorating those who perished, the memorial seeks to preserve the lived history of its victims while offering their families, the wider Jewish community, and the city a place for contemplation, mourning, and remembrance.

The design draws upon two enduring symbols of Jewish culture and faith: the *Menorah* and the *Tree of Life*. Their convergence establishes the memorial’s central architectural proposition, bringing together the historical weight of persecution and the enduring capacity for resilience, regeneration, and continuity.

Landscape is integral to this experience. The memorial is set within a tranquil environment intended to provide a contemplative counterpoint to the violence it commemorates. At the same time, the design acknowledges the railway networks that facilitated the systematic deportation of Jewish victims to concentration and extermination camps across Europe. The tracks become a material and spatial reference to the infrastructure through which the machinery of the Holocaust was executed.

Through these intertwined narratives of loss, memory, and survival, the memorial seeks to create a space that acknowledges the enormity of the atrocity while affirming the enduring significance of human dignity.

## Key facts

- Location: Lyon, France
- Organizer: Association pour l’édification d’un Mémorial de la Shoah à Lyon
- Typology: Memorial, Civic
- Status: Competition entry
- Year: 2023
- Material: Corten steel
- Resident architect: Sweetch Architects, Bordeaux
- Landscape architect: Ligne Paysagère, Versailles
- Structure: Web Structures, Ramboll
- 96 entries to the international competition, 2023
- 12.4 m height of the Corten steel sculpture
- 18 × 8 m memorial court of pools, rail tracks and benches
- 4 languages for the inscriptions on the memorial

## From the memory of atrocity to the resilience of life

The design departs from conventional memorial iconography by placing the resilience of victims and their families alongside the remembrance of suffering. Rather than relying exclusively on the visual language of tragedy, it proposes an architecture that holds loss and renewal in simultaneous tension. The memorial becomes both a record of historical atrocity and an expression of the collective capacity to remember, endure, and regenerate.

At its center, the *Tree of Life* emerges as a sculptural composition in Corten steel, formed through the overlapping geometries of the *Menorah* and the Tree of Life. The resulting form establishes an immediate visual identity while bringing together two complementary ideas: the enduring continuity of Jewish life and the collective act of remembrance. Its material presence is deliberately austere, allowing the sculpture to register as a powerful object within the landscape.

The memorial records its victims through the tattooed identification numbers assigned to them in the concentration camps. Where a number cannot be established, a blank line is proposed as a deliberate mark of absence—a reminder of the lives lost and the identities that history has failed to recover. This approach is subject to the competition’s restrictions on the representation of victims’ names and identification. If the use of tattooed numbers is not permissible, the lines may instead serve as a more abstract register of individual and collective loss.

## 

Water introduces a counterpoint to the permanence and austerity of the steel structure. A shallow, tiered fountain shaped around the Star of David feeds the linear watercourse, producing a gentle cascade that evokes continuity, renewal, and the persistence of life in the aftermath of tragedy.

Railway tracks are embedded within the paving, recalling the precise infrastructure through which thousands of Jewish victims were transported across Europe. Their physical presence establishes a direct connection between the memorial and the logistical systems that enabled mass deportation and extermination. Rather than functioning as incidental historical references, the tracks become part of the memorial’s spatial language, grounding its symbolism in the material reality of the Holocaust.

The project brings sculpture, water, landscape, and material history into a unified architectural proposition—one that confronts the memory of atrocity while affirming the possibility of resilience and renewal.

## Books

- 2026: Faire mémoire: 96 projets pour un mémorial, AAM Éditions (the pages on the project, PDF: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/press/books/2026-faire-memoire-lyon-shoah-memorial-tree-of-life.pdf)

# The Barn

Suretech House, Navi Mumbai. Navi Mumbai, India, 2026. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Barn transforms an industrial shed in Navi Mumbai into a contemporary workspace for Suretech Infrastructure, retaining elements of its original workshop, paint shop, and mechanical repair functions. Conceived alongside the client’s ambitions to rebrand and expand its business, the project demonstrates how a modest budget can become a catalyst for architectural reinvention. Rather than erasing the building’s industrial origins, the intervention builds upon its existing character, recalibrating its material expression and spatial organization to establish a renewed corporate identity.

## Key facts

- Location: Navi Mumbai, India
- Client: Suretech Infrastructure
- Typology: Adaptive reuse, Workplace
- Status: Completed
- Year: 2026
- Reuse an industrial shed adapted, not replaced
- Corten punched openings in a corrugated façade

## An industrial shell, reimagined

The building’s corrugated façade establishes a robust industrial presence, articulated by strategically placed apertures in Corten steel. Within, a contrasting palette of warm oak, exposed brick, and black powder-coated steel lends the workspace a sense of material warmth and refinement. The interplay between the rugged exterior and the carefully composed interior creates a distinct identity without resorting to an elaborate or resource-intensive transformation.

## A secondary spatial order

The intervention introduces a secondary layer of architectural articulation within the existing industrial shell. Corten steel apertures punctuate the corrugated envelope, while an internal cage of perforated steel establishes an additional spatial order. These elements mediate between enclosure and openness, preserving the building’s utilitarian character while adapting it to the demands of contemporary occupation.

The Barn demonstrates how an architecture of economy can deliver more than functional refurbishment: it can give a growing business a renewed identity, a stronger public presence, and a distinctive position within its market.

## Writing

- 2026 Jan: LinkedIn: The Barn, Suretech Infra, adaptive re-use (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/barn-suretech-infra-new-bombay-adaptive-re-use-mujib-ahmed-wadof)

## Credit for publications

# The Vessel

Jellyfish Water Sports Club, Kerala. Kerala, India. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Vessel transforms a modest, single-story village house on the banks of a tropical river in South India into guest facilities for the Jellyfish Water Sports Club. The project reinterprets the existing structure through a measured architectural intervention, expanding its capacity and strengthening its relationship with the river landscape. Rather than treating the original house as a constraint, the design uses its material and spatial qualities as the foundation for a new hospitality experience, shaped by the rhythms of the river and the maritime culture of its setting.

## Key facts

- Location: Kerala, India
- Client: Jellyfish Water Sports Club
- Typology: Adaptive reuse, Hospitality
- Status: Detailed design
- 1 village house of laterite and concrete, reused
- 2 floors: club dining and lounges below, guest rooms above

## A house that meets the river

The reconfigured program places dining and lounge spaces at ground level, with guest accommodation above. An extension expands the building’s footprint, while a swimming pool traces its perimeter beneath a sequence of terraces oriented toward the river. Together, these elements establish a continuous relationship between interior spaces, outdoor living, and the surrounding landscape. The river becomes more than a backdrop: it informs the organization of the spaces and the experience of inhabiting the building.

## A village house remade

The existing house, constructed in laterite stone and concrete and organized around modest rooms, is adapted to accommodate its new hospitality function. The intervention builds upon the material character of the original structure while reworking its spatial organization to support a more expansive and interconnected way of living.

The swimming pool winds around the building, following its perimeter and creating distinct zones for children and adults. Its sinuous geometry softens the relationship between the built form and the landscape, introducing movement into the composition while extending the experience of the house outdoors.

## Credit for publications

The Vessel, Kerala. Design: Collaborative Architecture (https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-vessel/)

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-vessel/

# Peace Pavilion

Indian National War (Peace) Museum, New Delhi. New Delhi, India, 2017. Design: Collaborative Architecture.

The Peace Pavilion was part of Collaborative Architecture’s finalist entry in the international competition for the Indian National War Museum in New Delhi, organized by the Government of India in 2017. Challenging the conventional narrative of a war museum, the studio proposed placing peace and nonviolence at the center of the national conversation on conflict, with a public pavilion that translated this proposition into an accessible civic space.

## Key facts

- Location: New Delhi, India
- Client: Government of India
- Typology: Museum, Civic
- Status: Finalist, two-stage international competition
- Year: 2017
- Exhibited: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York (June 2022 – September 2023); Museum of Craft and Design, San Francisco (October 2023 – February 2024)
- Collaborators: Arup; Landscape India; Suranjana Satewalker; Kapil Suralekar Associates; Shibu Raman (United Kingdom)
- 268 entries to the competition; one of seven practices in its final stage
- 40 projects from 25 countries in Designing Peace

## Reframing the narrative of war

The proposal questioned how a nation commemorates its military history, shifting the emphasis from conflict and victory toward the values of peace, nonviolence, and collective coexistence. Drawing on India’s philosophical and political traditions, from the teachings of the Buddha to Mahatma Gandhi’s vision of nonviolent resistance, the project advanced a broader understanding of national identity—one in which the history of war is inseparable from the pursuit of peace.

This conceptual reversal informed the architecture. The museum’s fortified mass was fragmented by crevices and double-curved glazing, tempering the symbolism of defense with a sense of openness. Arches and petal-like surfaces drew on the architectural vocabulary of Delhi’s historic monuments without reproducing them, establishing a contemporary expression rooted in cultural memory.

## A canopy for the city

Positioned within a public plaza between the street and the museum, the Peace Pavilion was conceived as an open civic threshold. Its perforated dome, inspired by the Buddhist stupa at Sanchi, evokes both a sacred architectural form and the canopy of a tree. Filtered daylight and shelter combine to create an inviting place for gathering, pause, and reflection.

A larger, ring-shaped canopy inscribed with a verse on peace from the Yajurveda extends this idea, establishing a public realm that remains accessible beyond the museum’s opening hours. The pavilion thus moves beyond the role of an architectural entrance to become a democratic space in its own right—one that invites people to gather irrespective of their purpose or relationship to the institution.

## Designing Peace

The proposal’s underlying premise—that architecture can advance peace by reshaping how societies understand and inhabit public space—led to its selection by the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum for Designing Peace, the fifth exhibition in its Humanitarian Design Series. Curated by Cynthia E. Smith with Caroline O’Connell, the exhibition brought together 40 projects from 25 countries to examine how design can help build and sustain peace.

The curatorial framing recognized the Peace Pavilion for reversing the premise of a national war museum competition, redirecting its emphasis toward peace as a cultural, civic, and political aspiration. The project was exhibited in New York from June 2022 to September 2023 and subsequently traveled to the Museum of Craft and Design in San Francisco, where it was shown from October 2023 to February 2024.

The competition attracted 268 entries, with Collaborative Architecture among seven practices to reach the final stage before the competition was shelved. The Peace Pavilion remains part of the studio’s continuing inquiry into *Architecture That Fosters Democracy*.

## Awards and shortlists

- 2017: Finalist, Indian National War Museum, two-stage international competition, Government of India

- 2023 Oct: Designing Peace, Museum of Craft and Design, San Francisco, October 7, 2023 – February 4, 2024 (https://sfmcd.org/exhibitions/designing-peace/)

<!-- https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/ -->

# Collaborative Lab

Speculative futures

Collaborative Lab is the studio’s research platform, investigating emerging questions through research, prototyping and policy advocacy to anticipate the forces shaping architecture in the decades ahead and translate these insights into practice.

## Design Policy for the State of Kerala

Strand: Policy Advocacy. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

### Design as a driver of development

Mujib Ahmed and Lalita Tharani, alongside Collaborative Lab’s research team, contributed to the development of a comprehensive design policy for Kerala. With its adoption, Kerala became the first state in India to establish a policy framework positioning design as a strategic instrument for shaping development priorities and guiding the state’s long-term trajectory.

- Partners: Government of Kerala

- Lead: Mujib Ahmed, Lalita Tharani, Lab research team

- Status: Adopted

- Partners: Government of Kerala

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-policy-advocacy-design-policy-for-the-state-of

## 1 × 1 | The Material Cartography of Contemporary Architecture in Bahrain

Strand: Architectural Cartographies, Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Proposed by Collaborative Lab for the Bahrain Pavilion at the 2027 Venice Biennale, 1 × 1 examines the material footprint of a single square meter of built space in Bahrain. Tracing the origins, logistics, energy, and embodied carbon of the materials that shape the country’s built environment, the research situates Bahrain’s material dependencies within a comparative regional framework measured against relevant United Nations climate benchmarks.

Moving beyond diagnosis, the proposal explores pathways toward a more resource-conscious architectural future—from adaptive reuse and resilient, adaptable buildings to innovative production processes, and the enduring intelligence of vernacular construction. It positions material choice as both an architectural decision and a strategic question of environmental responsibility, resource dependency, and the future of the built environment.

- Collaborators: Dr. Ardeshir Mahdavi, Dr. Christiane Berger, Dr. Wafa Alghatam

Project page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/material-cartographies/

## The Measured City | Hidden Cartographies of the UAE

Strand: Architectural Cartographies, Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

The Measured City is Collaborative Architecture’s proposal for the National Pavilion of the United Arab Emirates at the 2027 Venice Biennale. It positions the UAE as a laboratory for urban futures in arid regions, using data as a lens to examine how cities grow, function, and evolve. Moving beyond the familiar imagery of the region’s skylines, the exhibition maps decades of urban development across the emirates, examining livability, ecology, cultural continuity, and the networks that connect their cities. Through layered cartographies, it reveals patterns, achievements, and shortcomings that can inform future policy and design. An immersive spatial sequence invites visitors to encounter the UAE as a living, interconnected system—one whose hidden dynamics offer insights into the future of urbanism.

Project page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-measured-city/

## Project Alpha | Rethinking the Economics of Housing

Strand: Epistemologies. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Project Alpha is Collaborative Architecture’s entry to Initiative 99, ICON’s global challenge for affordable 3D-printed homes. The proposal questions whether construction efficiency alone can resolve the housing affordability crisis, recognizing that access to housing is shaped as much by land economics, finance, and regulation as by material and construction costs. It explores how additive manufacturing can contribute to affordability when supported by policy safeguards that address the wider forces shaping housing markets, including the risk of gentrification. Combining 3D-printed construction with familiar architectural forms, the proposal seeks to balance construction innovation with community acceptance.

### Replication with local adaptation

Designed for replication across communities with similar conditions, the housing system combines a consistent construction approach with adaptable interiors and shared public spaces. By balancing repeatability with spatial variation and collective amenities, Project Alpha explores how emerging construction technologies can support housing models that are economically accessible, socially responsive, and adaptable to diverse ways of living.

Project page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/project-alpha/

## Timber Mosques of Kerala | Architecture as Cultural Synthesis

Strand: Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Collaborative Lab documented a group of historic timber mosques in Kerala in collaboration with Professor K. T. Ravindran and a team led by conservation architect Savita Rajan. Tracing the architectural expression of Islam along Kerala’s historic trading coast, the research examines how early mosques emerged through an exchange between religious traditions and indigenous building practices. Rather than reproducing imported architectural forms, these structures evolved from local timber construction, craftsmanship, and spatial traditions, offering insight into how architecture mediates cultural exchange and acquires meaning through place and rootedness.

- Collaborators: Prof. K. T. Ravindran, Savita Rajan

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-design-research-timber-mosques-of-kerala-archi

## Project Brick | Reconsidering a Fundamental Building Material

Strand: Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Project Brick investigates the brick’s enduring influence on architectural form, urban development, and the relationship between cities and their hinterlands. As countries restrict traditional brickmaking to protect agricultural land and reduce emissions, the research examines how this ubiquitous material can evolve in response to environmental and resource constraints. It explores practices of material reuse, including *wapan*, popularized internationally through the work of architect Wang Shu, alongside cleaner production methods and the supply networks that connect urban construction to the landscapes that sustain it.

### From material tradition to circularity

By examining the connections between material production, reuse, and regional resource systems, Project Brick questions the linear processes through which cities consume and discard building materials. It seeks to identify pathways toward a more circular material economy, where established building traditions and emerging production methods inform a more resource-conscious architectural future.

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-design-research-project-brick-reconsidering-a-

## Design Audit of Kerala’s Public Schools | Evidence-Based Educational Infrastructure

Strand: Policy Advocacy. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Collaborative Lab, in collaboration with the Building Science Lab at the College of Architecture, Trivandrum, initiated the much-needed assessment with the Government of Kerala’s Department of Education to conduct a design audit of public schools across the state. The study maps existing facilities and evaluates the built environment as a basis for identifying opportunities for improvement. By establishing an evidence-based understanding of school infrastructure, the audit supports informed decisions on upgrading existing facilities and planning future schools.

- Partners: Department of Education, Government of Kerala; Building Science Lab, College of Architecture, Trivandrum

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-policy-advocacy-design-audit-of-kerala-s-publi

# Design Research, Collaborative Lab

Speculative futures

Collaborative Lab is the studio’s research platform, investigating emerging questions through research, prototyping and policy advocacy to anticipate the forces shaping architecture in the decades ahead and translate these insights into practice.

## 1 × 1 | The Material Cartography of Contemporary Architecture in Bahrain

Strand: Architectural Cartographies, Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Proposed by Collaborative Lab for the Bahrain Pavilion at the 2027 Venice Biennale, 1 × 1 examines the material footprint of a single square meter of built space in Bahrain. Tracing the origins, logistics, energy, and embodied carbon of the materials that shape the country’s built environment, the research situates Bahrain’s material dependencies within a comparative regional framework measured against relevant United Nations climate benchmarks.

Moving beyond diagnosis, the proposal explores pathways toward a more resource-conscious architectural future—from adaptive reuse and resilient, adaptable buildings to innovative production processes, and the enduring intelligence of vernacular construction. It positions material choice as both an architectural decision and a strategic question of environmental responsibility, resource dependency, and the future of the built environment.

- Collaborators: Dr. Ardeshir Mahdavi, Dr. Christiane Berger, Dr. Wafa Alghatam

Project page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/material-cartographies/

## The Measured City | Hidden Cartographies of the UAE

Strand: Architectural Cartographies, Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

The Measured City is Collaborative Architecture’s proposal for the National Pavilion of the United Arab Emirates at the 2027 Venice Biennale. It positions the UAE as a laboratory for urban futures in arid regions, using data as a lens to examine how cities grow, function, and evolve. Moving beyond the familiar imagery of the region’s skylines, the exhibition maps decades of urban development across the emirates, examining livability, ecology, cultural continuity, and the networks that connect their cities. Through layered cartographies, it reveals patterns, achievements, and shortcomings that can inform future policy and design. An immersive spatial sequence invites visitors to encounter the UAE as a living, interconnected system—one whose hidden dynamics offer insights into the future of urbanism.

Project page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-measured-city/

## Timber Mosques of Kerala | Architecture as Cultural Synthesis

Strand: Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Collaborative Lab documented a group of historic timber mosques in Kerala in collaboration with Professor K. T. Ravindran and a team led by conservation architect Savita Rajan. Tracing the architectural expression of Islam along Kerala’s historic trading coast, the research examines how early mosques emerged through an exchange between religious traditions and indigenous building practices. Rather than reproducing imported architectural forms, these structures evolved from local timber construction, craftsmanship, and spatial traditions, offering insight into how architecture mediates cultural exchange and acquires meaning through place and rootedness.

- Collaborators: Prof. K. T. Ravindran, Savita Rajan

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-design-research-timber-mosques-of-kerala-archi

## Project Brick | Reconsidering a Fundamental Building Material

Strand: Design Research. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Project Brick investigates the brick’s enduring influence on architectural form, urban development, and the relationship between cities and their hinterlands. As countries restrict traditional brickmaking to protect agricultural land and reduce emissions, the research examines how this ubiquitous material can evolve in response to environmental and resource constraints. It explores practices of material reuse, including *wapan*, popularized internationally through the work of architect Wang Shu, alongside cleaner production methods and the supply networks that connect urban construction to the landscapes that sustain it.

### From material tradition to circularity

By examining the connections between material production, reuse, and regional resource systems, Project Brick questions the linear processes through which cities consume and discard building materials. It seeks to identify pathways toward a more circular material economy, where established building traditions and emerging production methods inform a more resource-conscious architectural future.

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-design-research-project-brick-reconsidering-a-

# Policy Advocacy, Collaborative Lab

Speculative futures

Collaborative Lab is the studio’s research platform, investigating emerging questions through research, prototyping and policy advocacy to anticipate the forces shaping architecture in the decades ahead and translate these insights into practice.

## Design Policy for the State of Kerala

Strand: Policy Advocacy. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

### Design as a driver of development

Mujib Ahmed and Lalita Tharani, alongside Collaborative Lab’s research team, contributed to the development of a comprehensive design policy for Kerala. With its adoption, Kerala became the first state in India to establish a policy framework positioning design as a strategic instrument for shaping development priorities and guiding the state’s long-term trajectory.

- Partners: Government of Kerala

- Lead: Mujib Ahmed, Lalita Tharani, Lab research team

- Status: Adopted

- Partners: Government of Kerala

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/lab/#lab-policy-advocacy-design-policy-for-the-state-of

The study maps existing facilities and evaluates the built environment as a basis for identifying opportunities for improvement. By establishing an evidence-based understanding of school infrastructure, the audit supports informed decisions on upgrading existing facilities and planning future schools.

- Partners: Department of Education, Government of Kerala; Building Science Lab, College of Architecture, Trivandrum

# Epistemologies, Collaborative Lab

Speculative futures

Collaborative Lab is the studio’s research platform, investigating emerging questions through research, prototyping and policy advocacy to anticipate the forces shaping architecture in the decades ahead and translate these insights into practice.

## Project Alpha | Rethinking the Economics of Housing

Strand: Epistemologies. Led by Lalita Tharani and Mujib Ahmed, Collaborative Architecture.

Project Alpha is Collaborative Architecture’s entry to Initiative 99, ICON’s global challenge for affordable 3D-printed homes. The proposal questions whether construction efficiency alone can resolve the housing affordability crisis, recognizing that access to housing is shaped as much by land economics, finance, and regulation as by material and construction costs. It explores how additive manufacturing can contribute to affordability when supported by policy safeguards that address the wider forces shaping housing markets, including the risk of gentrification. Combining 3D-printed construction with familiar architectural forms, the proposal seeks to balance construction innovation with community acceptance.

### Replication with local adaptation

Designed for replication across communities with similar conditions, the housing system combines a consistent construction approach with adaptable interiors and shared public spaces. By balancing repeatability with spatial variation and collective amenities, Project Alpha explores how emerging construction technologies can support housing models that are economically accessible, socially responsive, and adaptable to diverse ways of living.

Project page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/project-alpha/

# Architecture in India

> Collaborative Architecture works across India from its Mumbai headquarters, with projects in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kerala, Delhi NCR, Hyderabad and Chennai.

Collaborative Architecture was founded in Mumbai, where it is headquartered, and has designed projects across India: schools and homes in Kerala, workplaces and experience centers in Bengaluru, research campuses and data centers in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, retail and pavilions in Delhi NCR, a river corridor with Henning Larsen in Hyderabad and a corporate office in Chennai. The studio takes on commissions in every metropolitan and tier 2 city.

# Architecture in the UAE

> Collaborative Architecture in the UAE: the Iconic Mosque for Emaar, the Bearys Wafira residences, The Souk for Dubai Design Week; all seven emirates.

The studio’s work in the United Arab Emirates began in Dubai, with The Souk, a prize-winning timber pavilion for Dubai Design Week 2019, the Iconic Mosque, and the Bearys Wafira residences and experience center. The studio takes on commissions in all seven emirates and across the Gulf, where it has also worked in Bahrain and Qatar. For the 2027 Venice Biennale, it proposed The Measured City for the National Pavilion of the United Arab Emirates, an exhibition that maps decades of urban development across the emirates.

# Architecture in Saudi Arabia

> Collaborative Architecture SA, the Riyadh studio, serves clients in Riyadh, Jeddah, the Eastern Province and the giga-project regions of Saudi Arabia.

Collaborative Architecture SA is the studio’s office in Riyadh. It brings the Mumbai studio’s experience of workplaces, cultural buildings, hospitality and narrative environments to clients across the Kingdom, from Riyadh and Jeddah to the Eastern Province and the giga-project regions. The Cliff Chair and the Ripple jewelry collection take their forms from the murals and eroded landscape of AlUla. From Riyadh, the studio also serves clients across the GCC, Egypt and Morocco.

# Architecture in Bahrain

> Collaborative Architecture in Bahrain: The Iconic Gateway for Diyar Al Muharraq, and 1 × 1, a material cartography proposed for Bahrain’s pavilion at the 2027 Venice Biennale.

Collaborative Architecture’s work for Bahrain spans civic infrastructure and research. For Diyar Al Muharraq, the studio designed The Iconic Gateway, a pedestrian bridge and landmark that marks the entrance to the new city, drawing on Bahrain’s maritime heritage and the interlocking arches of the Diyar identity. For the Kingdom’s national participation at the 2027 Venice Biennale, Collaborative Lab proposed 1 × 1, which traces the materials, energy and embodied carbon of a single square meter of Bahrain’s built space and the pathways toward a more resource-conscious architecture. The studio serves Bahrain from Riyadh and Mumbai.

## Projects

- [The Iconic Gateway](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-gateway/): Muharraq, Bahrain, 2023, Infrastructure
- [Material Cartographies](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/material-cartographies/): Venice, Italy, 2026, Exhibition, Research

## Where we work in Bahrain

### Governorates

- Capital: Manama
- Muharraq: Muharraq, Diyar Al Muharraq
- Northern: Hamad Town, Budaiya
- Southern: Riffa, Sakhir

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/in/bahrain/

# Architecture in Mumbai

> Collaborative Architecture in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai: a sea-facing apartment at Cuffe Parade, a research campus, a data center and an industrial conversion.

Collaborative Architecture is headquartered in Mumbai and has worked across the city and in Navi Mumbai: Apartment by the Bay, a 180-square-meter home overlooking the sea at Cuffe Parade; Wedge-1, an installation for Stanley; Prototype N[ON] for Moroso; the BGRT Mumbai research campus; a data center for NTT Data; and The Barn, an industrial shed converted into a workspace for Suretech Infrastructure.

## Projects

- [Wedge-1](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/wedge-1/): Mumbai, India, 2009, Retail
- [BGRT Mumbai](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/bgrt-mumbai/): Navi Mumbai, India, In design, Research campus
- NTT Data Center: Navi Mumbai, India, Three phases completed, Digital infrastructure
- [The Barn](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-barn/): Navi Mumbai, India, 2026, Adaptive reuse
- [Prototype N[ON]](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/prototype-non/): Mumbai, India, 2008, Retail, Exhibition
- [Apartment by the Bay](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/apartment-by-the-bay/): Mumbai, India, 2014, Residential

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/in/mumbai/

# Architecture in Bengaluru

> Collaborative Architecture in Bengaluru (Bangalore): the Reflected Topography lobby, the MillerKnoll Experience Center, an NTT Data center and Rasa Totem.

In Bengaluru the studio designed Reflected Topography, the public lobby of the Bearys Global Research Triangle, lit by 53 custom lights set into its waffle slab; the MillerKnoll Experience Center, a net-zero experience center; a data center for NTT Data; and Rasa Totem, a 20-meter sculpture with the artist Riyas Komu, proposed for the new terminal of Kempegowda International Airport.

## Projects

- [Reflected Topography](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/reflected-topography/): Bengaluru, India, 2014, Workplace
- [MillerKnoll Experience Center](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/miller-knoll-experience-center/): Bengaluru, India, 2025, Experience center
- [Rasa Totem](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/rasa-totem/): Bengaluru, India, 2022, Art installation
- NTT Data Center: Bengaluru, India, 2019, Digital infrastructure

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/in/bengaluru/

# Architecture in Kerala

> Eleven projects in Kochi, Kozhikode and across Kerala: show apartments for Skyline Builders and PVS Developers, schools, homes, restaurants and showrooms.

Kerala is where the studio has built most: eleven projects in Kochi, Kozhikode and across the state. They include Stacked Tectonics, a primary school built by village workers; Inverted Topography, the Mezban restaurant; House of Cantilevers, a family villa; Wrap-4 for KTC Hyundai; and The Legend, a show condominium in Kochi. The principals also contributed to the Design Policy for the State of Kerala, the first such policy adopted by an Indian state.

## Projects

- [Stacked Tectonics](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/stacked-tectonics/): Kozhikode, India, 2012, Education
- [Inverted Topography](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/inverted-topography/): Kozhikode, India, 2010, Hospitality
- Parallel House: Kerala, India, 2013, Residential
- [House of Cantilevers](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/house-of-cantilevers/): Kerala, India, Under construction, Residential
- [Wrap-3](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/wrap-3/): Kozhikode, India, 2006, Education
- [Wrap-4](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/wrap-4/): Kerala, India, 2007, Retail
- [The Legend](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-legend/): Kochi, India, 2018, Residential
- [50th Cross Road](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/50th-cross-road/): Kerala, India, 2020, Residential
- iRooms: Kozhikode, India, Under construction, Hospitality
- Aafco Experience Center: Kerala, India, Under construction, Experience center
- [The Vessel](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-vessel/): Kerala, India, In design, Adaptive reuse

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/in/kerala/

# Architecture in Delhi NCR

> Collaborative Architecture in New Delhi and Delhi NCR: the Stanley Lifestyle Store, Peace Pavilion for the National War Museum and Concept Pavilion II.

In Delhi NCR the studio designed the Stanley Lifestyle Store; Peace Pavilion, its finalist proposal in the competition for the Indian National War Museum, later exhibited in New York and San Francisco; and Concept Pavilion II for Titan. The Stanley store presents the brand’s home and workplace collections across about 2,300 square meters. Lalita Tharani’s installation Levitation was shown at the DX Show in New Delhi in 2019.

## Projects

- [Peace Pavilion](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/peace-pavilion/): New Delhi, India, 2017, Museum, Civic
- Concept Pavilion II: New Delhi, India, 2006, Retail
- [Stanley Lifestyle Store](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/stanley-lifestyle-store/): Delhi NCR, India, 2009, Retail

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/in/delhi-ncr/

# Architecture in Dubai

> Collaborative Architecture in Dubai: The Souk for Dubai Design Week, the Iconic Mosque for Emaar, and the Bearys Wafira residences and experience center.

In Dubai the studio designed The Souk, a cluster of three timber pods around a small square that won the installation program of Dubai Design Week in 2019, and a competition design for a new mosque for Emaar, conceived as a civic landmark and a center for tolerance. It also designed the Bearys Wafira residences and the Bearys Wafira Experience Center. In the Gulf it has worked in Bahrain and Qatar, and its Riyadh studio, Collaborative Architecture SA, serves clients in Saudi Arabia.

## Projects

- [Iconic Mosque](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/iconic-mosque/): Dubai, UAE, 2018, Religious
- [The Souk](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/the-souk/): Dubai, UAE, 2019, Pavilion
- [Bearys Wafira](https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/bearys-wafira/): Dubai, UAE, Due 2029, Residential
- Bearys Wafira Experience Center: Dubai, UAE, Under construction, Experience center

Page: https://collaborativearchitecture.com/work/in/dubai/
